docs.title: PoreFM
docs.text:
A foundation model for nanopore signal and sequence.

PoreFM uses raw electrical signal and nucleotide sequence to detect DNA and RNA modifications and compare samples.

Run the RNA example Install Models

docs.title: Choose an analysis
docs.text:
Your goal Method Control sample at inference Result Call modifications with a fine-tuned classifier Supervised detection No Trained class calls and probabilities Call a broader set of modifications using learned prototypes Prototype joint footprinting No Supported modification calls and relative scores Find departures from canonical signal expectations Zero-shot detection No Anomaly scores and p-values Compare a sample with a matched control Pairwise comparison Yes Embedding shifts and test-read anomaly scores

Supervised models use a classifier trained on labelled data. Prototype models learn modification prototypes from small labelled datasets and use footprinting to account for neighboring effects. Both use contextual PoreFM representations. The released prototype models cover more modification types, including some without a supervised model; see the model catalog.

The released models include their trained components; no model training or prototype fitting is needed to follow these inference guides. Zero-shot detection is also called de novo detection: it flags departures from a canonical model without assigning a modification identity.

Choose a release matching your sequencing chemistry: RNA004 or DNA R10.4.1 (E8.2, 400 bps). The model catalog lists the modifications supported by each classifier and prototype model.

All four methods produce read-level results that can be summarized at reference sites. Anomaly fractions, class-call fractions, and mean probabilities measure different quantities; see output interpretation.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
1. Install PoreFM.
  2. Run the HeLa RNA example for a first result and a comparison of all four methods.
  3. Prepare your own inputs and follow the relevant analysis guide.
  4. Summarize and explore your results without loading a model.

For custom analyses, export per-base embeddings. For questions, citations, and license information, see project information.

docs.title: Zero-shot detection and output filtering
docs.text:
For a complete application recipe with matching null, whitening, scale, and calibration artifacts, start with zero-shot detection. This page covers additional modes and output options.

porefm zero-shot detect scores read positions using a unified canonical reference model and empirical k-mer calibration. It supports cosine and whitening scores, with the score family selected from calibration metadata by default. Supply the matching whitening artifact for whitening detection.

docs.title: Single-file model bundles
docs.text:
Use --model-path RNA004_zero-shot.pt (or --model_path) to provide all model artifacts in one file. This overrides --canonical_null_model_path, --calibration_path, and --whitening_artifact, even if those paths are invalid. Set input, output, filtering, and device options on the detection command.

Create a bundle once from matching artifacts:

porefm utils bundle-model --kind zero-shot \
  --canonical_null_model_path scale/model.best \
  --calibration_path calibration.pt \
  --whitening_artifact whitening.pt \
  --output RNA004_zero-shot.pt

porefm zero-shot detect --model-path RNA004_zero-shot.pt \
  --bam_path aligned.signal.bam --ref reference.fa \
  --motif 'N 0' --output_dir predictions/aligned

Whitening can be omitted when packaging cosine-only detection. The destination must not exist. A bundle contains all required inference components; the source files are not needed on the inference machine. Load it with the detection command, rather than torch.load. Inference verifies component checksums and extracts temporary files under TMPDIR (or the system temporary directory). Allow enough disk space for the complete component set; these temporary files are cleaned up when inference exits.

Detection always writes paired data/meta Parquets, factoring out repeated read names, chromosomes, and strands. Read these files and collapse them to reference loci with porefm.outputs.open_output; see the shared output API for filters, DuckDB, and streamed site summaries.

docs.title: Optional deterministic execution
docs.text:
Add --deterministic to porefm zero-shot detect to request repeatable numerical execution for identical inputs, model artifacts, batching, hardware, and software versions. Compilation remains enabled unless --disable_compile is also supplied; autocast and matmul precision follow the command settings.

This option enables PyTorch deterministic algorithms, fixes numerically sensitive compiler kernel choices, disables cuDNN benchmarking, and defaults CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG to :4096:8 when it is unset. PyTorch raises an error for operations it identifies as lacking a deterministic implementation. The requested option and effective numerical settings/software versions are recorded in run_manifest.json under arguments.deterministic and arguments.numerical_policy.

Deterministic execution can be slower and can produce different scores and p-values from the default policy. It does not retrain the model, refit whitening, or regenerate calibration. When using an existing calibration, assess p-value behavior on canonical controls before relying on thresholds under the selected policy. The option applies only to detection. Identical results across devices, versions, or batch layouts are not guaranteed.

docs.title: Aligned, reference-based inference
docs.text:
Omit --chrom to process eligible aligned reads across all reference contigs. Specify --chrom chr1 chr2 to restrict the run. This mode still requires a reference FASTA and aligned inputs. Signal-BAM input requires coordinate sorting and indexing; direct BAM + POD5 uses its read-ID index instead (see input preparation). Motifs/position labels are reference-based; --motif "N 0" selects all aligned bases without constructing a genome-wide label dictionary.

porefm zero-shot detect \
  --bam_path aligned.signal.bam \
  --canonical_null_model_path scale/model.best \
  --calibration_path calibration.pt \
  --whitening_artifact whitening.pt \
  --ref reference.fa \
  --motif "N 0" \
  --output_dir predictions/aligned

docs.title: Unaligned or mixed aligned/unaligned samples
docs.text:
Use --read_based (also spelled --read-based). Without --chrom, this streams BAM records in file order, including unmapped reads, without requiring a BAM index or reference FASTA. It selects motifs in the called sequence, not the reference. --motif "N 0" selects every eligible canonical read base; it is expanded into A/C/G/T motifs per read, not reference-wide arrays.

porefm zero-shot detect \
  --bam_path unaligned.signal.bam \
  --canonical_null_model_path scale/model.best \
  --calibration_path calibration.pt \
  --whitening_artifact whitening.pt \
  --read_based --motif "N 0" \
  --output_dir predictions/read_based

Sequence type, pore chemistry, and k-mer currents come from checkpoint metadata. Use matching model, whitening, and calibration artifacts. Raw signal is required, either in SG tags or supplied with --pod5. Move tables are preferred; supported chemistries can infer chunks when moves are absent. Ordinary basecalls alone are not sufficient.

  • readname and zero-based read_pos identify observations. Unmapped reads have chrom="*", position=-1, and strand=-1. Do not group these rows by reference position as though they were genomic sites.
  • Supplying --ref in read-based mode retains available reference coordinates for aligned reads. Without it, reference positions are unavailable even for mapped records; the BAM contig name/strand may still be recorded.
  • An explicit --chrom restricts read-based mode to aligned records on those contigs and requires --ref (plus a coordinate index for signal-BAM input). Omit it to include unmapped reads. Supplying only --ref does not impose a chromosome filter.
  • Read-based mode requires --motif and cannot use --pos_file. Reference- guided polishing requires --ref and suitable aligned reads; it is not an unaligned-read operation.
  • Flag, read-length, quality, valid-kmer, trimming, and score filters apply. --max_batches, if supplied, limits the run. “All reads” removes chromosome restriction; it does not disable these filters.

Read-based mode is explicit rather than auto-enabled when --ref is absent, so an accidentally omitted reference cannot silently change motif semantics.

docs.title: P-value filtering and peak output
docs.text:
porefm zero-shot detect supports an inclusive p-value cutoff and optional peak finding. Add these options to an existing inference command with its usual model, calibration, input, and output paths:

--motif "N 0" --max_pvalue 0.01 --peak_only --prune_radius 5
  • --max_pvalue P writes only finite p-values <= P, with P in [0, 1]. It replaces the raw-distance filter, so explicitly combining it with --min_metric is an error. This option works independently of peak finding and can be used with motif/position selections.
  • --peak_only reports local p-value minima after overlapping chunks have been stitched into a read. It requires all-base selection (--motif "N 0") and no --pos_file. It works in both reference-based and read-based modes.
  • --prune_radius W optionally suppresses weaker qualifying peaks within +/- W read bases, inclusive. For W=5, retained peaks must be at least 6 bases apart. The default, 0, disables pruning; a positive radius requires --peak_only. Distance uses read_pos, not genomic coordinates, including for reverse-strand, spliced, and unmapped reads.

Peak finding uses the original p-values, before applying the chosen output threshold. Each peak or equal-valued plateau must have valid, strictly higher p-values on both sides. Flat peaks use their midpoint rounded down: positions 100--104 select 102, while 100--103 select 101, not 100. Invalid k-mers, unlabelled bases, nonfinite p-values, and missing positions break the profile; their neighboring segment endpoints are not called as peaks. Gaps are never compressed away. Chunk trimming determines available bases.

After peak detection, the selected p-value or raw-distance cutoff is applied. If distance pruning is enabled, qualifying peaks are considered by increasing p-value, with lower read position breaking ties. Each retained peak suppresses its neighbors; suppressed peaks cannot suppress other peaks. Results are written in read-position order with their original scores and p-values. For example, peaks at 100, 104, and 108 with p-values 0.001, 0.002, and 0.003 and radius 5 retain 100 and 108. A smoothly declining shoulder is not a peak.

These options select output rows after scoring and calibration. Without either threshold, the default distance > 0.0 filter applies. Without --peak_only, all qualifying bases are emitted. No smoothing or prominence filter is applied. Small secondary peaks can survive, and distance pruning can merge distinct nearby modifications.

docs.title: Wider sequence context
docs.text:
Add --output_context_radius 15 to porefm zero-shot detect to save 31 bases around each retained position:

--motif "N 0" --max_pvalue 0.01 --peak_only --prune_radius 5 \
--output_context_radius 15

The default radius is 0 (disabled). A positive radius R adds sequence_context and boolean context_complete. Context works with either output threshold, with or without peak finding, and with motif/position selections. It adds context to the selected rows without rescoring them.

Context follows the model-input sequence, in read orientation, including on reverse-strand reads. With --use_polished_sequence, this is the polished sequence and its read coordinates, which can differ from original BAM query offsets. The alphabet is A/C/G/T/N, including T for RNA, consistent with the k-mer column. The reported base is at zero-based context index R. Available neighboring bases are included even if they are unlabelled, trimmed from scoring, or fail the output filter. Overlapping chunks use the same midpoint stitching as the scores.

Unavailable read flanks or gaps between loaded chunks are padded with N, and context_complete is false. An observed N counts as available and does not by itself make context incomplete. No extra BAM/reference lookup is made to fill gaps; context cannot recover sequence absent from the loaded chunks.

docs.title: Compact storage and decoding
docs.text:
The default --output_context_format packed stores lossless binary DNA: two bits per A/C/G/T base plus an N mask only for contexts containing N. A 31-base context takes 8 bytes, or 12 bytes with an N mask, before Parquet overhead and compression. The output reader decodes packed contexts automatically when the column is selected:

from porefm.outputs import open_output

calls = open_output("outputs/zero-shot")
for table in calls.iter_tables(
    columns=["readname", "read_pos", "sequence_context", "context_complete"],
    reads_per_batch=32,
):
    print(table.to_pandas().head())

Use --output_context_format text to store directly readable DNA strings. Keep the same format and radius across parts of one dataset. See the output API for filtering and selecting columns without loading the whole run into memory.

docs.title: Classifier precision and logit regularization
docs.text:
Final classifier projections run in float32 in both training and inference, even inside bfloat16 autocast. Transformer heads use float32 for their final two-layer GELU projection; CNN heads use float32 for the final linear layer. The backbone and the attention/convolutional head body use the configured autocast policy.

Supervised cross-entropy, focal, exclusion, proportion, and logit-penalty calculations use float32. --logit_reg_lambda weights mean(logits.square()) over all retained bases and classes. The raw penalty equals the centered penalty plus the mean squared per-base logit offset. It therefore constrains growth in a shared offset that leaves ideal softmax probabilities unchanged but can erase class differences when low-precision logits become large. Changing the penalty coefficient is not a substitute for computing the projection and loss with sufficient precision.

Supervised checkpoints record logit_regularization: raw_mean_square, classifier_projection_dtype: float32, and supervised_loss_dtype: float32 in their training metadata. A coefficient of zero disables the penalty. Assess numerical stability on representative data when choosing training settings.

docs.title: CLI and configuration reference
docs.text:
This guide explains how PoreFM command-line values are parsed and documents the configuration-file formats consumed by maintained commands. Command help is the source of truth for individual flags and current defaults:

porefm
porefm <command> --help

Running porefm or a leaf command with no additional arguments prints help and exits successfully. Choices appear next to their option in braces, and defaults appear in the option description when a meaningful default is set.

The maintained BAM and source configs described below use strict JSON contracts. Validate a file without starting a model or opening BAMs with:

porefm utils validate-config validate /path/to/config.json
porefm utils validate-config validate /path/to/config.json --show-normalized
porefm utils validate-config validate /path/to/supervised.json --class-labels C 5mC 5hmC
porefm utils validate-config schema pretraining

The validator rejects duplicate or unknown fields, wrong types, unsupported schema versions, and invalid relationships between fields. --show-normalized displays the effective config after optional defaults are applied. Pass --class-labels for supervised configs to validate class names and indices against their CLI order. Supported schema names are pretraining, bam-sharding, and supervised. Validation checks the config contract, not whether paths exist or whether BAM/FASTA contents are compatible. Structural validation uses the emitted Draft 2020-12 schemas; a small semantic layer applies defaults and checks relationships involving external CLI values.

Paths in the examples are placeholders; replace them with your own inputs and output destinations.

docs.title: Find the relevant options
docs.text: Task Reference Supply samples to inference; use POD5 or exclude reads Inference inputs Define supervised labels, class metadata, or supervision Supervised labels and training inputs Change signal chunk boundaries Signal chunking Configure pretraining modality dropout Signal dropout during training

docs.title: Command-line value syntax
docs.text:
The shell splits arguments before PoreFM sees them. Follow these conventions:

  • Multi-value options using nargs are whitespace-separated. A comma does not separate list items. For example:
--bam_config control.json modified.json
--class_labels canonical 5mC 5hmC
--num_loss_trim 16 32
  • A value that itself contains spaces must be quoted so it remains one argument. Motif sets are the common case:
--motif_string 'CG 0;CH 0'
--motif 'DRACH 2;CG 0'
  • Do not write --chrom chr1,chr2 for an option whose help says it accepts multiple values. Use --chrom chr1 chr2. Commas may still be part of one value's own syntax, as in --mods C:m,h A:a; explicitly documented single-string options may also accept comma-delimited content.
  • Paths containing spaces must also be quoted.
  • CLI booleans are flags such as --disable_compile; do not append true or false unless the help explicitly declares a value.

For distributed pretraining or fine-tuning, continue to use module mode because TorchRun launches a Python module on every rank:

torchrun --module porefm.cli.finetune_modification [options]

docs.title: Configuration formats at a glance
docs.text:
Format Used by Top-level structure Pretraining JSON porefm pretrain, porefm zero-shot train, train-scale, fit-whitening, calibrate, auxiliary supervised pretraining Object containing samples BAM-sharding JSON porefm utils shard-bam --bam_config Object containing inputs Supervised/inference BAM JSON porefm finetune-modification, porefm detect-modification Object containing labelled_samples or tagged_samples Canonical-null pipeline manifest and stage JSON Written by porefm zero-shot pipeline Output records; do not use as hand-written input configs

Include config_type and schema_version in each input JSON, as shown in the examples below. Use one object per sample or input in the appropriate array.

docs.title: Pretraining and canonical-null JSON
docs.text:
Use this format with --bam_config for pretraining and direct canonical-null training/calibration. Supervised auxiliary pretraining accepts one or more of these files through --pretrain_bam_config.

{
  "config_type": "pretraining",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "samples": [
    {
      "bam_path": "/path/to/control.bam"
    },
    {
      "bam_path": "/path/to/modified.bam",
      "sampling_probability": 0.5
    }
  ]
}

Rules and strict assumptions:

  • samples is required and must be a nonempty array.
  • Each sample requires bam_path.
  • sampling_probability is optional and defaults to 1.0. It must be a finite number in (0, 1] and independently controls whether each eligible BAM record is retained. It is not a relative source or class weight.
  • Unknown sample and top-level fields are rejected.
  • Paths are used as written; environment variables and ~ are not expanded by the parser.
  • For DDP, provide enough independent BAM files or shards for the configured rank/worker topology.
  • Pretraining polishing remains run-wide: use --use_polished_sequence, --polish_indel_limit, and --polish_vcf_path. Per-sample polishing fields are deliberately not accepted because the current pretraining dataset uses one polishing policy for the entire run.

The canonical-null pipeline takes one config in this format, creates disjoint sample-level pretraining JSON configs, and passes the generated configs to its stages. Split provenance and fractions are recorded in pipeline_manifest.json.

docs.title: BAM-sharding JSON
docs.text:
Use this format with porefm utils shard-bam --bam_config:

{
  "config_type": "bam-sharding",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "inputs": [
    {
      "bam_path": "/path/to/sample1.bam",
      "contigs": ["chr1", "chr2"]
    },
    {
      "bam_path": "/path/to/sample2.bam"
    }
  ]
}

Rules:

  • inputs is required and must be a nonempty array.
  • Each input requires bam_path.
  • contigs is an optional array of unique nonempty strings and defaults to [], which processes all records/contigs.
  • Sampling probabilities are not accepted by this schema.
  • Alternatively, use --bam_path for one BAM and omit --bam_config.
  • Inputs selected by contig require coordinate-addressable aligned BAMs.

docs.title: Generated canonical-null JSON
docs.text:
porefm zero-shot pipeline writes:

  • pipeline_manifest.json, recording inputs, deterministic split counts, artifacts, and stage states;
  • stage_args/<stage>.args.json, recording the exact effective arguments for each stage.

These files are provenance outputs, not supported hand-written input schemas. Do not edit them to resume or alter a run; use the pipeline's reuse/output options and retain the generated manifest with the artifacts.

docs.title: Preflight checklist
docs.text:
Before a large analysis:

  1. Validate JSON with porefm utils validate-config validate CONFIG.json and check the command's --help for available options.
  2. Check input paths and the indexes needed by your input route:
Input route Signal and indexing requirements Direct BAM + POD5 inference Matching read IDs; a .pfmi index is built automatically. A coordinate BAM index is unnecessary. Reference-based SG BAM, pairwise comparison, or explicit SG contig selection Raw signal in SG; sorted, indexed alignments and a matching indexed FASTA. Unscoped read-based SG BAM Raw signal in SG; coordinate sorting and a BAM index are unnecessary.
  1. Preserve sequence and quality information. Keep mv move tables and signal trimming tags when available; pod5-to-bam requires mv. Supported 9-mer chemistries can infer chunks without moves, while RNA002 requires moves. For move-based decoding, check the stride against the checkpoint's ts_dim.
  2. When reference coordinates are needed, check that BAM and FASTA contig names and lengths agree. Reference-guided polishing additionally needs suitable alignments with CIGAR and MD information.
  3. For training, verify class order across labels, position-file columns, modification codes, and model outputs.
  4. Keep the command, input configs, model version, and run manifest with results.

docs.title: Pairwise sample comparison
docs.text:
Start with the test-versus-control recipe for a complete command and output summary. This page describes the available options.

porefm pairwise-comparison compares control and test samples directly from BAM inputs.

The workflow compiles the model with torch.compile(dynamic=True) by default. --disable-compile selects eager execution for diagnostics.

Unless --step is supplied explicitly, BAM collection chooses a downstream chunk step from --size: DNA reserves 128 time steps of overlap and RNA reserves 256. Windows too small for the normal overlap use a step equal to three quarters of their size. The resolved choice is printed before data collection; the small augmentation stride recorded by a pretraining checkpoint is intentionally ignored.

docs.title: Analysis modes
docs.text:
Mode Control retained Test retained Parquet scores BAM output --sitewise-embedding-shift Per-site count and sum Per-site count and sum Mean-embedding MSE and cosine distance per locus No --sitewise-anomaly-scoring All canonical rows All canonical rows Per-test-read MSE, cosine distance, retained PC scores, squared Mahalanobis distance, and p-value; separate per-site PCA/null statistics Anomaly Phred or control-mean cosine --readwise-anomaly-scoring Per-site count and sum All canonical rows Per-test-read MSE and cosine distance against the full control mean Control-mean cosine

sitewise-anomaly-scoring already includes each test read's direct comparison with its sitewise control mean, so it cannot be selected together with readwise-anomaly-scoring. sitewise-embedding-shift may be combined with either read-scoring mode when both locus-level and read-level outputs are needed. The minimum control and test coverage defaults are 15. Readwise scoring requires the control threshold but intentionally permits one test read at a site; the test threshold applies to the two sitewise modes.

All modes use the same ownership rule for overlapping model windows. Each eligible read position is assigned to the chunk in which it lies furthest from a real sequence edge; equal-margin ties use the earlier chunk. Thus a read position contributes at most one embedding, regardless of mode.

For sitewise anomaly scoring, each test row stores exactly pc_1 through pc_N, where N is --n-components. These are the coordinates actually used for its squared Mahalanobis distance: a separate control-standardized, joint PCA space is fitted for every position and strand. Direct MSE and cosine distance remain in the original selected embedding space.

docs.title: Direct BAM input
docs.text:
porefm pairwise-comparison \
  --model-path model.pt \
  --control-bam control.bam \
  --test-bam test.bam \
  --ref reference.fa \
  --motif-string "A 0" \
  --sitewise-anomaly-scoring \
  --sitewise-embedding-shift \
  --output comparison_run

Use sorted, indexed signal BAMs with SG tags. Sequence type, pore chemistry, and expected k-mer currents are inferred from the model checkpoint.

When either population expands to more than one BAM, its layout must be declared explicitly:

  • ordered-shards naturally sorts numeric shard suffixes and reads the files as an ordered coordinate stream within each worker assignment.
  • independent-streams performs a k-way merge of independently sorted BAM streams.

Pass --exclude-bed excluded.bed to skip reads overlapping unwanted regions before signal decoding, chunking, and embedding accumulation. This applies to both populations, including --store-embeddings, and defaults to disabled. The file accepts three or four whitespace-separated columns:

# chrom start end strand
chr9 3000000 3100000
chr9 5000000 5100000 -

Coordinates are zero-based and half-open. Three-column rows exclude both strands. Optional column 4 must be + or - and is matched to the BAM alignment strand, also for RNA. Rows with and without strand may be mixed. Chromosome names must match the BAM exactly. A matching overlap discards the entire read from collection, including its positions outside the region. The reference span includes introns and deletions; touching endpoints do not overlap. Blank lines and # comments are allowed. This is a custom four-column strand extension to BED3, not standard BED4 with a name column or BED6 with strand in column 6.

Use --num-workers 4 for up to four loader processes per population, or set --control-num-workers 4 --test-num-workers 4 independently. The shared default is 1 per population. An override of 0 reads that population in the main process. Negative counts are rejected. Each positive request is capped at the number of unique expanded BAM paths in that population; one BAM uses at most one worker. Requested/effective counts are logged, and effective counts are recorded in the run manifest.

--prefetch-factor defaults to 2 complete-read batches per worker and applies only to subprocess loading. --reads-per-chunk controls reads per buffer; --forward-batch-size separately caps model chunks per forward pass. Independent streams also retain one batch per active BAM inside each worker, so their memory use depends on the BAM count as well as the worker/prefetch settings. Worker count changes can change batching and capped fit-sample selection; they preserve complete-read ownership and observation counts, not bitwise score reproducibility.

Use --store-embeddings to export embeddings in genomic blocks while the BAMs are being processed. A classifier checkpoint is also accepted; the selected backbone embedding is still used for comparison.

docs.title: Classifier filtering
docs.text:
With a classifier checkpoint in --model-path, control and test can use independent allowed class indices and probability thresholds. For example, add:

  --control-filter-class-index 1 2 \
  --control-filter-min-probability 0.95 0.96 \
  --test-filter-class-index 0 2 \
  --test-filter-min-probability 0.90 0.98

Indices are zero-based classifier output columns, using the label mapping of that checkpoint. Each index is paired with the threshold in the same list position. Both options must be supplied together for a population, with equal nonzero list lengths, unique nonnegative indices, and finite thresholds in [0, 1].

A control position in this example passes when P(class 1) >= 0.95 or P(class 2) >= 0.96; test positions independently require P(class 0) >= 0.90 or P(class 2) >= 0.98. Probabilities use softmax over all classifier classes. They are not summed or renormalized over allowed labels, and a passing class does not have to be the highest-probability class. Passing multiple thresholds still retains the position only once. Omit both options for a population to leave it unfiltered.

Filtering selects individual read positions after canonical chunk ownership is fixed. Rejected positions do not fall back to other overlapping chunks. Coverage thresholds, means, anomaly fits, scores, and exported embeddings all use the retained positions. Annotated BAMs still contain the original records; only retained, eligible positions receive comparison scores. Both populations use the same checkpoint.

Run manifests record both filters. Resuming a run requires the same labels and thresholds for both populations.

docs.title: Performance and reproducibility
docs.text:
Reduce --forward-batch-size for GPU memory pressure. Loader workers are assigned per population and capped by the number of BAM files; increasing workers for a single BAM does not increase parallelism. Prefetching and independent input streams also consume host memory.

Changing worker counts or processing order can change the capped fit-sample selection and resulting scores. For repeatable comparisons, keep inputs, settings, software, device, and processing order fixed. Background output writes finish before successful completion or BAM annotation; write errors fail the run.

docs.title: Outputs and BAM support
docs.text:
• locus_metrics/*.parquet stores sitewise embedding shifts.
  • read_scores/*_meta.parquet stores readname, reference, strand, and the number of contiguous rows in the corresponding data table.
  • read_scores/*_data.parquet stores flattened positions and scores in metadata-row order. This is the same per-read meta/data factoring used by classifier inference. Sitewise anomaly rows also contain pc_1 through pc_N; their repeated site coverage is moved to anomaly_site_metrics instead of being duplicated here. Readwise direct scoring retains coverage in this table because it does not fit a PCA/null site table.
  • anomaly_site_metrics/*.parquet stores one row per eligible position and strand for sitewise anomaly scoring. It records full control/test coverage, capped PCA-fit coverage, scored-test coverage, empirical-calibration coverage, and the control mean and regularized covariance in PCA space. control_pca_covariance is flattened row-major into a fixed-size list.
  • embeddings/*.pt stores versioned canonical control and test rows when --store-embeddings is selected. Row embeddings are compact bfloat16, while float32 site means and counts are stored separately. Enabling export does not change the mean-based scores computed during BAM processing. These files are available for downstream analysis; the CLI does not rescore them.

For BAM annotation, pass --annotated-bam-dir, --bam-base, --bam-mod-code, and one of these score selections:

Add --drop-tags SG mv to remove raw signal and move-table tags from every annotated output record, including records without scores. Removal happens after scoring and polishing; omitting this option retains those tags.

--bam-base is emitted as the MM fundamental base after uppercasing. RNA mode does not rewrite T as U, so pass --bam-base T for consumers such as IGV that require thymine in RNA BAM modification tags. Pass U explicitly when uracil output is desired.

  • --bam-score anomaly-phred converts each p-value to Q = -10 log10(p), then writes round(255 * clip(Q / --bam-phred-max, 0, 1)). The default --bam-phred-max 40 maps p-values 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001 to approximately 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% intensity. It requires --sitewise-anomaly-scoring.
  • --bam-score control-mean-cosine writes scaled cosine distance and works with either read-scoring mode.

The selected byte score is written to the standard ML array and duplicated in ES by default. CV contains byte-clipped site coverage, and MM/MN describe the encoded sites and sequence length. MSE remains Parquet-only. Source test BAMs are re-read for annotation, so the mean-only sitewise-embedding-shift mode cannot produce BAM output. When test sequence polishing is enabled, the annotated BAM uses the same polished sequence and coordinate maps used during embedding collection.

--chrom-list restricts both populations during scoring and restricts annotated BAM records to mapped alignments on those references. Indexed annotation inputs fetch only the selected references, in BAM header order; unindexed inputs are filtered during a sequential scan. Selected records without scores are still copied. Unmapped records are excluded when a chromosome list is supplied. Without a chromosome restriction, annotation copies all source records. Output headers retain the full reference dictionary.

docs.title: Annotating calibrated canonical-null Parquet
docs.text:
Canonical-null comparison writes flat per-read rows containing readname, chrom, position, strand, and pvalue. Annotate these without rerunning the model using:

python -m porefm.cli.pairwise_parquet_to_bam \
  --bam input.bam --parquet canonical_null_output/ \
  --output_bam annotated.bam --base N --mod_code N --seq_type dna \
  --canonical_null

This mode writes Phred-40-scaled ML bytes: round(255 * clip(-10 log10(p) / 40, 0, 1)). It writes no coverage tag and removes existing CV and cv tags from every output record, even with --preserve_existing_mod_tags. calibration_count is not read coverage and is never copied into a coverage tag. Coverage-column overrides and --require_coverage are rejected in this mode. Pairwise square-root encoding is the default when --canonical_null is omitted. Use --chrom_list chr2 to restrict output to mapped records on selected references in indexed BAM inputs. Without this option, the flat-Parquet annotator copies the entire input BAM. Add --drop_tags SG mv to remove signal and move-table tags from output records. The compact-score annotation Python API supports the same removal through drop_tags=("SG", "mv"). Other input tags are retained apart from the score and coverage tags replaced or removed by the selected annotation mode.

docs.title: First result: HeLa RNA
docs.text:
Run PoreFM on a small RNA004 dataset covering COL5A1: native HeLa RNA (WT) and an in-vitro-transcribed control (IVT). This walkthrough downloads the inputs, runs four analysis methods, and plots their outputs in the same 200-base window.

Follow installation first. The commands below use a CUDA GPU, curl, gzip, and samtools. Run the Bash blocks in order in a terminal. For a first result, complete the download and supervised sections; the remaining methods extend the comparison. The Python plotting blocks are optional and expandable. Run them in order in one Python session, or use the downloadable plotting script below.

docs.title: What you will need and produce
docs.text:
Item Details Hardware Linux and a CUDA GPU supported by FlashAttention 2; see installation. Input A COL5A1 subset of native HeLa RNA and an IVT control, their POD5 signals, and a GRCh38 chromosome 9 reference. First result Separate BAMs and prediction Parquets from the m6A/inosine and pseU supervised models, plotted together. Full walkthrough Four plots and small site-summary tables for the same 200-base window. Storage Keep space for downloads, the decompressed FASTA, cached models, and inference outputs; pairwise comparison also creates signal BAMs.

Model compilation makes the first run slower. Runtime and memory use depend on the GPU, batching, and installed software. If GPU memory is limiting, use the resource settings in the individual analysis guides.

docs.title: Download the example data
docs.text:
The files are public in WGLab/PoreFM_examples. This URL pins the dataset revision used for the figures; no Hugging Face account or package is needed. The WT/IVT data are from:

Yongji Zou, Mian Umair Ahsan, Joe Chan, Wen Meng, Shou-Jiang Gao, Yufei Huang, and Kai Wang. A comparative evaluation of computational models for RNA modification detection using nanopore sequencing with RNA004 chemistry. Briefings in Bioinformatics 26(4), bbaf404 (2025). doi:10.1093/bib/bbaf404.

mkdir -p porefm-hela/data
cd porefm-hela

DATA_URL=https://huggingface.co/datasets/WGLab/PoreFM_examples/resolve/063aaa1e8ddc92705f04cd58af09fe4643869fae/hela_RNA_example
for file in GRCh38.chr9.fa.gz \
  HeLa_WT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam HeLa_WT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam.csi HeLa_WT.pod5 \
  HeLa_IVT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam HeLa_IVT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam.csi HeLa_IVT.pod5; do
  curl --fail --location --retry 3 "$DATA_URL/$file" --output "data/$file"
done

gzip -dc data/GRCh38.chr9.fa.gz > data/GRCh38.chr9.fa
samtools faidx data/GRCh38.chr9.fa

The BAMs provide basecalls and alignments; their matching POD5 files provide the raw signal. The FASTA supplies reference coordinates. The first three methods read BAM + POD5 directly. Pairwise comparison uses signal BAMs, which we create below.

Models download automatically through --model ...@v0.1.0 and are reused from the local cache. See Models for cache settings and offline prefetching. Use fresh output directories when rerunning inference. The first run can take longer while models compile.

docs.title: Call m6A, inosine, and pseU with supervised models
docs.text:
Run two classifiers on the WT sample: one for A/m6A/inosine and one for U/pseU. Each model has its own target base and output directory.

porefm detect-modification \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine@v0.1.0 \
  --bam_path data/HeLa_WT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam --pod5 data/HeLa_WT.pod5 \
  --ref data/GRCh38.chr9.fa --read_based --motif 'A 0' \
  --output_format both \
  --output outputs/supervised

A 0 selects A bases in each called read. The model distinguishes canonical A, m6A, and inosine; its checkpoint supplies chemistry settings and BAM modification codes. both writes Parquets and outputs/supervised/output.bam with MM/ML modification tags.

Then call pseudouridine with the pseU model:

porefm detect-modification \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_pseU@v0.1.0 \
  --bam_path data/HeLa_WT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam --pod5 data/HeLa_WT.pod5 \
  --ref data/GRCh38.chr9.fa --read_based --motif 'T 0' \
  --output_format both \
  --output outputs/supervised-pseu

T 0 selects uridine bases, encoded as T in the BAM sequence. This model distinguishes U and pseU; its checkpoint supplies BAM base T and pseudouridine modification code 17802. Outputs go to outputs/supervised-pseu, including a separate output.bam.

The BAMs are unsorted because input follows POD5 traversal. Prepare copies for a genome viewer:

samtools sort -o outputs/supervised/calls.sorted.bam outputs/supervised/output.bam
samtools index outputs/supervised/calls.sorted.bam
samtools sort -o outputs/supervised-pseu/calls.sorted.bam outputs/supervised-pseu/output.bam
samtools index outputs/supervised-pseu/calls.sorted.bam

docs.title: Inspect the Parquets
docs.text:
Keep the checkpoint_*_data.parquet and checkpoint_*_meta.parquet files together. open_output joins predictions with their read identities and coordinates for you:

from porefm.outputs import open_output

supervised = open_output("outputs/supervised")
print(supervised.class_labels)  # ('A', 'm6A', 'Ino')
print(supervised.schema.names)
preview = next(supervised.iter_tables(
    columns=["readname", "chrom", "position", "predicted_class",
             "prob_m6A", "prob_Ino"],
    batch_size=5,
))
print(preview.to_pandas().to_string(index=False))

pseu = open_output("outputs/supervised-pseu")
print(pseu.class_labels)  # ('U', 'pseU')
preview = next(pseu.iter_tables(
    columns=["readname", "chrom", "position", "predicted_class", "prob_pseU"],
    batch_size=5,
))
print(preview.to_pandas().to_string(index=False))

docs.title: Reference annotations
docs.text:
PoreFM tables use zero-based reference positions. We select chr9:[134843446, 134843646) on the forward strand (strand=0), and display one-based positions on the plots: 134,843,447–134,843,646.

The highlighted sites are reference annotations, not targets supplied to the models:

Position on plot (1-based) Modification Reference assay Assay percentage 134,843,485 Pseudouridine (pseU) BACS 15.6% 134,843,496 m6A GLORI 71.6% 134,843,607 m6A GLORI 64.1%

Reference assays:

  • GLORI (m6A): Liu C, Sun H, Yi Y, Shen W, et al. Absolute quantification of single-base m6A methylation in the mammalian transcriptome using GLORI. Nat Biotechnol. 2023;41(3):355–366. PMID:36302990.
  • BACS (pseudouridine): Xu H, Kong L, Cheng J, et al. Absolute quantitative and base-resolution sequencing reveals comprehensive landscape of pseudouridine across the human transcriptome. Nat Methods. 2024;21(11):2024–2033. doi:10.1038/s41592-024-02439-8.

These assay percentages provide reference measurements. PoreFM call fractions and anomaly fractions have different definitions and are not interchangeable with those measurements. The three sites are also available as a tab-separated table.

docs.title: Reproduce the plots
docs.text:
Download the plotting script into your porefm-hela directory. After both supervised runs complete, run:

python plot_results.py --method supervised

Use --method prototype, --method zero-shot, or --method pairwise after running that method, or --method all after all four. The script needs no GPU. It writes or replaces the derived files in plots/ and summaries/.

To work interactively instead, expand the Python blocks below and run this shared setup once. It adds the same site markers to every figure.

Shared Python plotting setup (run once) 
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

Path("plots").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("summaries").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
START, END = 134843446, 134843646
region = [("chrom", "==", "chr9"), ("position", ">=", START),
          ("position", "<", END), ("strand", "==", 0)]
truth = [(134843484, "pseU", "#009988"),
         (134843495, "m6A", "#CC3311"),
         (134843606, "m6A", "#CC3311")]

def finish_plot(fig, axes, title, filename):
    """Label genomic tracks and save a figure using one-based display positions."""
    axes = np.atleast_1d(axes)
    for ax in axes:
        for position, label, color in truth:
            ax.axvline(position + 1, color=color, linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
        ax.set_xlim(START + 1, END)
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
        ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.2)
        ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda x, _: f"{x:,.0f}"))
    for i, (position, label, color) in enumerate(truth):
        axes[0].text(position + 1, 1.04 + 0.10 * (i == 1), label,
                     transform=axes[0].get_xaxis_transform(),
                     ha="center", color=color, fontsize=10)
    axes[-1].set_xlabel("GRCh38 chr9 coordinate (1-based)")
    axes[0].set_title(title, loc="left", pad=48, fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(f"plots/{filename}.png", dpi=180, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()

docs.title: Plot per-site m6A, inosine, and pseU percentages
docs.text:
Each summary assigns a prediction its most probable class. The m6A and inosine percentages use all called A-family observations as their denominator; the pseU percentage uses all called U-family observations. Canonical A and U calls stay in their respective denominators. Keep the two summaries separate, since the models score different bases. Retain sites with at least 20 called observations within each model to avoid large percentages from a handful of basecalling errors at other reference bases.

Python: summarize and plot supervised calls 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.8))
runs = [
    ("supervised", [("m6A", "m6A", "#CC3311"),
                    ("Ino", "Inosine", "#4477AA")]),
    ("supervised-pseu", [("pseU", "pseU", "#009988")]),
]
for directory, classes in runs:
    calls = open_output(f"outputs/{directory}")
    sites = calls.summarize_loci(
        filters=region, include_class_counts=True,
    ).sort_values("position")
    sites.to_parquet(f"summaries/{directory}.parquet", index=False)
    plot_sites = sites[sites.called_count >= 20]
    columns = ["position", "called_count"] + [f"freq_{label}" for label, _, _ in classes]
    print(directory, plot_sites[columns].head())
    for label, name, color in classes:
        ax.scatter(plot_sites.position + 1, 100 * plot_sites[f"freq_{label}"],
                   s=18, label=name, color=color)
ax.set(ylabel="Modification calls (%)", ylim=(-3, 103))
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)
finish_plot(fig, ax, "Supervised calls · HeLa WT / COL5A1", "supervised")

The two annotated m6A sites stand out among the A-family calls, while inosine calls are low in this window. The pseU track comes from the separate U/pseU classifier. At the annotated pseU site, it calls 33 of 301 U-family observations as pseU (11.0%); the BACS assay reports 15.6%. These are distinct measurements, as described above. The plot illustrates this region and does not establish genome-wide accuracy.

docs.title: Call modifications with prototypes
docs.text:
The prototype model learns modification prototypes from small labelled datasets and uses footprinting to account for neighboring effects when calling modifications. This released RNA model supports m6A, inosine, m5C, pseU, and 2′-O-methylated A/C/G/U, including modification types without a released supervised classifier. Run it on the same WT BAM + POD5:

porefm prototype classify \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0 \
  --bam_path data/HeLa_WT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam --pod5 data/HeLa_WT.pod5 \
  --ref data/GRCh38.chr9.fa --read_based --motif 'N 0' \
  --effect_penalty 50 \
  --output_dir outputs/prototype

N 0 scores all eligible bases. The penalty of 50 belongs to this RNA recipe; it is not a significance threshold. Outputs are part_* Parquets plus effect_parts.json and effect_run.json; keep them together.

Plot every modeled modification class in a different color. Here each class count is divided by all called observations at the genomic site, including canonical calls. This gives one common per-site denominator across classes.

Python: summarize and plot prototype calls 
prototype = open_output("outputs/prototype")
print(prototype.class_labels)
prototype_sites = prototype.summarize_loci(
    filters=region, include_class_counts=True,
).sort_values("position")
prototype_sites.to_parquet("summaries/prototype.parquet", index=False)
modifications = [label for label in prototype.class_labels
                 if label not in {"A", "C", "G", "T", "U"}]
colors = {"m6A": "#CC3311", "Inosine": "#4477AA", "2OmeA": "#EEAA33",
          "m5C": "#228833", "2OmeC": "#AA3377", "2OmeG": "#66CCEE",
          "pseU": "#009988", "2OmeU": "#8844AA"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.3))
for label in modifications:
    ax.scatter(prototype_sites.position + 1, 100 * prototype_sites[f"freq_{label}"],
               s=19, alpha=0.8, color=colors[label], label=label)
ax.set(ylabel="Modification calls (%)", ylim=(-3, 103))
ax.legend(loc="upper right", ncol=4, frameon=False, fontsize=8)
finish_plot(fig, ax, "Prototype calls · HeLa WT / COL5A1", "prototype")

The prototype model can assign classes across base families, including pseU. The example shows m6A calls near both annotated m6A sites and a smaller pseU signal near its annotation. Inspect competing calls and coverage as well as the largest class fraction; the scores are not calibrated probabilities.

docs.title: Find anomalies with the zero-shot model
docs.text:
This method flags departures from canonical RNA without requiring an IVT control or assigning a modification identity.

porefm zero-shot detect \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_zero-shot@v0.1.0 \
  --bam_path data/HeLa_WT.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam --pod5 data/HeLa_WT.pod5 \
  --ref data/GRCh38.chr9.fa --read_based --motif 'N 0' \
  --max_pvalue 1 \
  --output_dir outputs/zero-shot

--max_pvalue 1 retains both significant and nonsignificant calls so the per-site denominator is complete. The following plot shows the percentage of scored reads with p ≤ 0.01, followed by p-values along one read. The API calls this fraction fraction_modified; here it is an anomaly-call fraction, not a chemical identity or calibrated modification stoichiometry.

Choose a read with the most scored positions in this window (read-name order breaks ties). This selects for coverage, without selecting on its p-values. The p-value axis is logarithmic, with smaller values toward the top.

Python: summarize and plot zero-shot anomalies 
denovo = open_output("outputs/zero-shot")
denovo_sites = denovo.summarize_loci(
    filters=region, modified_pvalue_cutoff=0.01, combine_pvalues=False,
).sort_values("position")
denovo_sites.to_parquet("summaries/zero-shot.parquet", index=False)
read_calls = pd.concat([
    table.to_pandas() for table in denovo.iter_tables(
        columns=["readname", "position", "pvalue"], filters=region,
    )
], ignore_index=True)
coverage = read_calls.groupby("readname").position.nunique().rename("positions").reset_index()
readname = coverage.sort_values(["positions", "readname"], ascending=[False, True]).iloc[0].readname
one_read = read_calls[read_calls.readname == readname].sort_values("position")
print("Example read:", readname, "scored positions:", len(one_read))
one_read.to_parquet("summaries/zero-shot-read.parquet", index=False)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 6), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(denovo_sites.position + 1, 100 * denovo_sites.fraction_modified, color="#284B63")
axes[0].set(ylabel="Anomaly calls (%)", ylim=(-3, 103))
axes[1].plot(one_read.position + 1, one_read.pvalue.clip(lower=1e-8),
             color="#4477AA", marker=".", markersize=3)
axes[1].axhline(0.01, color="#777777", linestyle="--", label="p = 0.01")
lower = min(0.001, max(1e-8, one_read.pvalue.min()))
axes[1].set(yscale="log", ylim=(1, lower), ylabel="One-read anomaly p-value")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
finish_plot(fig, axes, "De novo detection · HeLa WT / COL5A1", "zero-shot")

Zero-shot detection highlights departures from the canonical model. The fraction depends on the p-value threshold and can differ substantially from supervised class fractions. Peaks may extend to neighboring bases because nanopore signals reflect sequence context. The single read illustrates local scores; it is not a site-level estimate.

docs.title: Compare WT with the IVT control
Convert to signal BAMs
docs.text:
Pairwise comparison uses sorted BAMs containing SG raw-signal tags. Attach POD5 signals to each population, then sort and index the resulting BAMs:

mkdir -p signal
for sample in WT IVT; do
  porefm utils pod5-to-bam \
    --bam "data/HeLa_${sample}.COL5A1.GRCh38.bam" \
    --input "data/HeLa_${sample}.pod5" \
    --output signal --prefix "${sample}.unsorted" --threads 4
  samtools sort -o "signal/${sample}.bam" "signal/${sample}.unsorted.bam"
  samtools index "signal/${sample}.bam"
done

docs.title: Run pairwise comparison
docs.text:
porefm pairwise-comparison \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA@v0.1.0 \
  --control-bam signal/IVT.bam --test-bam signal/WT.bam \
  --ref data/GRCh38.chr9.fa --chrom-list chr9 \
  --sitewise-embedding-shift --sitewise-anomaly-scoring \
  --output outputs/pairwise

The first scoring option compares mean WT and IVT embeddings. The second scores individual WT reads against the IVT population. Sites need at least 15 retained observations in each population with the default settings.

Plot cosine distance between mean embeddings and the percentage of WT reads with p ≤ 0.01. The latter is again an anomaly-call fraction.

Python: summarize and plot pairwise results 
pairwise = open_output("outputs/pairwise")
pairwise_sites = pairwise.summarize_loci(
    filters=region, modified_pvalue_cutoff=0.01,
).sort_values("position")
shifts = pd.concat([
    table.to_pandas() for table in pairwise.iter_site_tables(
        kind="locus_metrics", filters=region,
    )
], ignore_index=True).sort_values("position")
pairwise_sites.to_parquet("summaries/pairwise.parquet", index=False)
shifts.to_parquet("summaries/embedding-shifts.parquet", index=False)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 6), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(shifts.position + 1, shifts.cosine_distance, color="#284B63")
axes[0].set(ylabel="Mean-embedding\ncosine distance", ylim=(0, None))
axes[1].plot(pairwise_sites.position + 1, 100 * pairwise_sites.fraction_modified, color="#284B63")
axes[1].set(ylabel="WT anomaly calls (%)", ylim=(-3, 103))
finish_plot(fig, axes, "Pairwise WT vs IVT · COL5A1", "pairwise")

Both tracks show changes near the annotated sites, using the measured IVT control instead of a fitted canonical reference. Nearby bases can share a signal footprint, so the largest shift need not land exactly on the modified base. These tracks identify differences between populations without assigning a chemical modification identity.

docs.title: Keep the results
docs.text:
plots/ contains the four figures, and summaries/ contains the small per-site tables used to draw them. To inspect a saved summary later:

print(pd.read_parquet("summaries/supervised.parquet").head())
print(pd.read_parquet("summaries/supervised-pseu.parquet").head())

Each inference directory also contains run_manifest.json, recording model versions, checksums, input settings, and software provenance. The figures above use the displayed commands and the pinned dataset/model versions. For larger analyses and additional output queries, see processing outputs and the individual analysis guides.

docs.title: Model compilation defaults
docs.text:
Model-executing CLI commands use torch.compile(model, dynamic=True). The first run can take longer while kernels compile; use the opt-out below to diagnose compilation failures.

CLI Default Opt-out / notes pairwise-comparison Compiled --disable-compile prototype extract-kmer-prototypes Compiled --disable_compile; union and model-free dry runs execute no model pretrain Compiled --disable_compile finetune-modification Compiled --disable_compile detect-modification Compiled --disable_compile zero-shot train, train-scale, fit-whitening, calibrate Compiled --disable_compile zero-shot pipeline Compiled Passes --disable_compile to its model stages zero-shot detect Compiled --disable_compile; optional --deterministic fixes numerically sensitive kernel choices prototype classify Compiled backbone --disable_compile

Commands that process stored embeddings, plots, BAM tags without a model, or configuration files have no model to compile.

zero-shot detect --deterministic retains compilation and the command precision settings, but opts into deterministic PyTorch kernels. It can change runtime speed and numerical rounding relative to the default execution policy. The option applies to detection. See the detection guide for reproducibility limits and calibration considerations.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Browse all releases in the PoreFM collection on Hugging Face. Choose the model for your sequencing chemistry and analysis method.

docs.title: RNA
docs.text:
Chemistry: RNA004. Backbone embedding dimension: 512.

Model on Hugging Face Version Checkpoint files Description PoreFM-RNA 0.1.0 backbone.pt, pretraining.pt Pretrained RNA backbone for embeddings, pairwise comparison, and downstream training; also available with pretraining heads. PoreFM-RNA_zero-shot 0.1.0 RNA004_zero-shot.pt Canonical-null model with whitening and calibration for detecting deviations from canonical RNA signals. PoreFM-RNA_prototype 0.1.0 RNA004_prototype.pt Prototypes learned from small labelled datasets, with joint footprinting for m6A, inosine, m5C, pseudouridine, and 2′-O-methylated A/C/G/U. PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine 0.1.0 model.pt Supervised classifier distinguishing canonical A, m6A, and inosine. PoreFM-RNA_pseU 0.1.0 model.pt Supervised classifier distinguishing canonical U and pseudouridine (pseU).

docs.title: DNA
docs.text:
Chemistry: R10.4.1 (E8.2, 400 bps). Backbone embedding dimension: 384.

Model on Hugging Face Version Checkpoint files Description PoreFM-DNA 0.1.0 backbone.pt, pretraining.pt Pretrained DNA backbone for embeddings, pairwise comparison, and downstream training; also available with pretraining heads. PoreFM-DNA_zero-shot 0.1.0 R10.4.1_zero-shot.pt Canonical-null model with whitening and calibration for detecting deviations from canonical DNA signals. PoreFM-DNA_prototype 0.1.0 R10.4.1_prototype.pt Prototypes learned from small labelled datasets, with joint footprinting for 5mC, 5hmC, and 6mA. docs.title: Choosing a checkpoint
docs.text:
For modification identities, choose a supervised classifier or a prototype model that includes your target classes. Supervised models use classifiers trained on labelled data. Prototype models learn prototypes from small labelled datasets and use footprinting to account for neighboring effects. Both use contextual PoreFM representations. The released prototype models cover more modification types, so a modification can have a prototype model even when no supervised model is available.

  • backbone.pt contains the pretrained backbone for embeddings, pairwise comparison, and downstream tasks.
  • pretraining.pt contains the same backbone plus pretraining objective heads and the EMA target encoder. Optimizer and scheduler states are excluded.
  • Zero-shot and prototype bundles contain their required backbone and fitted components; separate model-component paths are unnecessary.
  • Supervised model.pt files contain the backbone, classifier, preprocessing, class labels, and base/modification-code defaults.

Derived models use the corresponding RNA or DNA pretrained backbone and include the weights needed for inference. A separate base-model download is unnecessary when using a derived model.

docs.title: Downloading and using models
docs.text:
Use --model OWNER/REPOSITORY@vVERSION to download a published release automatically. The version is part of the same argument; there is no separate version option. An explicit tag such as @v0.1.0 is required.

porefm prototype classify \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0 \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ --ref reference.fa \
  --chrom chr1 --motif 'N 0' \
  --effect_penalty 50 \
  --output_dir outputs/prototype

The four inference commands select the appropriate artifact from the release:

Command Example model argument Artifact selected detect-modification --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine@v0.1.0 Complete supervised classifier. zero-shot detect --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_zero-shot@v0.1.0 Complete canonical-null bundle. prototype classify --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0 Complete prototype bundle. pairwise-comparison --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA@v0.1.0 Pretrained backbone; supervised classifier releases can also supply embeddings and class filtering.

For supervised pseudouridine detection, use --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_pseU@v0.1.0 with --read_based --motif 'T 0'. Its class labels are U and pseU; RNA uridine is represented as T in BAM sequences and modification tags. The checkpoint supplies SAM modification code 17802. The HeLa example runs both RNA supervised models.

Downloads use public HTTPS file URLs with Python's standard library. No Hugging Face package, CLI, account, or login is required for these public releases. PoreFM reads manifest.json, pins the checkpoint download to the resolved repository commit, and verifies its size and SHA-256 before use. It never silently substitutes the latest release for a missing version.

docs.title: Cache directory
docs.text:
The default cache is ~/.cache/porefm/models, or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/porefm/models when XDG_CACHE_HOME is set. Configure a shared cache through the environment:

export POREFM_MODEL_CACHE=/path/to/shared/porefm-models

Alternatively, add --model-cache-dir /path/to/cache to an inference or download command. This option takes precedence over the environment variable. PoreFM verifies cached checkpoint checksums and reuses valid files without contacting the server. Concurrent processes sharing a cache coordinate downloads. The cache is independent of Hugging Face's SDK cache.

docs.title: Prefetching and offline use
docs.text:
Download on a machine with internet access before launching a GPU job:

porefm models download \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0 \
  --model-cache-dir /path/to/shared/porefm-models

The command prints the verified local checkpoint path to stdout; download progress goes to stderr. On the compute node, use the same --model and cache directory, adding --offline to prohibit network access. A missing or corrupt cached model then produces an error.

Base-model repositories default to backbone.pt. Request the pretraining checkpoint explicitly when needed:

porefm models download --model WGLab/PoreFM-DNA@v0.1.0 --file pretraining.pt

docs.title: Local files and reproducibility
docs.text:
Load local checkpoints with --model-path or --model_path. Use either a local path or --model, not both. Local paths never trigger a download, and can point to files obtained manually or through another cache. For training, pass the prefetched checkpoint path to the training command's checkpoint-loading option.

For --model runs, run_manifest.json records the requested model reference, version, resolved repository commit, selected filename, checkpoint SHA-256, and release-manifest SHA-256 under model_source. The local checkpoint path is also recorded. This provenance is retained when using cached models offline.

For setup and examples, see inputs and models, supervised detection, zero-shot detection, pairwise comparison, and prototype-based joint footprinting.

docs.title: Checkpoint checksums
docs.text:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
