docs.title: Reading and summarizing PoreFM outputs
docs.text:
For a short introduction with previews and links to workflow-specific summaries, start with processing output files.

porefm.outputs provides one entry point for read-level calls and reference-site summaries. It runs without loading a model or allocating a GPU. Analysis dependencies are included in the standard PoreFM installation.

from porefm.outputs import open_output

calls = open_output(output_dir)  # format="auto" by default
print(calls.format, calls.schema)
Format Accepted layout Basic site summary canonical_null Paired part_*_data.parquet / part_*_meta.parquet Valid p-value counts, anomaly fractions, Fisher combined p-value pairwise Comparison run with read_scores/ P-value counts and anomaly fractions prototypes Effect manifest plus family-local data/meta, or per-k-mer classifier parts Hard-call frequencies and called/total counts supervised checkpoint_* or rank_*_checkpoint_* data/meta Argmax frequencies and called/total counts

Directories are inspected nonrecursively. Comparison roots automatically select read_scores/; sibling site statistics are not treated as read observations. Flat input can also be a file, glob, or explicit file list. Split file paths resolve their companions. Mixed layouts and inconsistent schemas raise errors. Use one inference/comparison run per dataset. Rows are not deduplicated.

Common logical column names are readname, chrom, position, read_pos, strand, and pvalue where available. Stored refname, refpos, read_position, and p_value/p_val are renamed to those common names. Other fields retain their producer names and precision. Reference positions are zero-based, strand is 0 forward/1 reverse, and read coordinates retain the producer's orientation. No reference coordinates are inferred for unmapped positions. Negative positions remain visible in read-level output.

For SQL queries, specialized pairwise diagnostics, and label selection, see advanced output analysis.

docs.title: Filtered read-level access
docs.text:
For a single read, a set of read IDs, or a preview:

filters = {
    "readname": ["read-id-1", "read-id-2"],
    "call_status": "called",
    "predicted_class": ["A", "6mA"],
}

for table in calls.iter_tables(
    columns=["readname", "chrom", "position", "read_pos", "predicted_class"],
    filters=filters,
    reads_per_batch=128,
):
    process(table)  # release each batch before advancing

Canonical-null, prototype and supervised readers default to 32 complete stored reads per batch. Set reads_per_batch=N to change this; rows and RAM usage vary with read length. Metadata length values define split-file records. Filtering keeps all matching stored rows of a read together; it does not restore bases excluded during inference. Reads with no matches do not count toward the batch size. Batches may span parts; only the final batch has fewer reads. Repeated read names from duplicate inputs or separate alignments are not merged.

For strict row limits use batch_size=N instead (mutually exclusive with reads_per_batch). Pairwise readers retain row batching, default 65,536 rows, because genomic-block files can divide a read across parts; reads_per_batch is not supported for pairwise output. DuckDB views do not impose read order.

Filters combine with AND; a list value means any of those values. An empty list selects no rows. Filter fields need not appear in columns. Classification filters apply only to formats that have class calls; use pvalue, chrom, readname, etc. for null/pairwise results. Unknown column names raise. A class label absent from the dataset matches no rows in the common API.

Comparison operators use a list of triples:

filters = [
    ("chrom", "==", "chr1"),
    ("position", ">=", 1_000_000),
    ("position", "<", 1_100_000),
    ("pvalue", "<=", 0.05),
]

Supported operators are ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, in, not in. Use == None/!= None for nulls. NaN is distinct from null. Both Arrow and native SQL filters use Arrow's NaN comparison semantics: ordered comparisons and equality to finite values are false; inequality is true. Selecting only needed columns reduces decoding and memory use. Metadata for one part is also held in memory. No-match results retain their schema.

For medium datasets, load Arrow once and convert to pandas once:

import pandas as pd

table = calls.read_table(columns=columns, filters=filters)
df = table.to_pandas(types_mapper=pd.ArrowDtype)

Arrow concatenation shares batch buffers. All selected data still needs to fit in RAM; do not accumulate batches if the dataset is too large. Packed null sequence_context is decoded to text only when selected. Pass decode_context=False to retain packed bytes and their encoding/length metadata.

Supervised calls derive predicted_class, probability, and call_status from stored prob_* columns. All stored logits/probabilities remain available. Ties pick the first stored class; any missing, nonfinite or out-of-range probability makes the row unavailable_context. Prototype score families are expanded with nulls for inapplicable classes. Prototype output provides scores, not probabilities.

docs.title: Inspect an active job
docs.text:
calls = open_output(output_dir, allow_incomplete=True)

This snapshots finished pairs. Reopen to include later parts. Prototype effect manifests provide completion and stale-file checks. Other split layouts do not have a completion manifest: strict mode requires both files for every discovered stem; incomplete mode skips unpaired stems. A footer/schema error is surfaced, not silently skipped. The supervised writer does not publish atomically, so retry opening if its current file is still being written. Do not restart or overwrite an input directory while a reader is using it.

docs.title: Collapse reference loci without loading all reads
docs.text:
sites = calls.summarize_loci(
    filters={"call_status": "called"},  # classification formats
    classes=["A", "6mA", "C", "5mC", "5hmC"],
    memory_limit="8GB",
    threads=4,
)

# Or stream only the aggregated site batches to a separate Parquet file:
calls.summarize_loci(
    output_path=site_output_path,
    memory_limit="8GB",
    temp_directory=spill_directory,
    threads=4,
)

All summaries exclude position < 0 (including -1 and -2), missing/* chromosomes, and strands other than 0/1. Default grouping is chrom, position, strand. An entirely reference-free run therefore returns an empty site table. DuckDB aggregates across parts without retaining the full read table in Python. Only site batches cross into Python. Memory limits govern DuckDB operations, not every allocation or the size of a returned pandas table. Keep site output outside the read-part directory so it cannot be mistaken for another input part. Existing outputs require overwrite=True; input part files cannot be overwritten by the shared summary function.

Summaries process read data in parts and may use temporary disk space under temp_directory (or the system temporary directory). Temporary files are cleaned up automatically. Millions of final loci can still form a large pandas table; use output_path to write the final site batches directly to Parquet.

Classification summaries return total_count, called_count, and freq_LABEL. The denominator is all retained non-null class calls, including classes not listed in classes. That option chooses report columns, not a filter. Filtering to modified classes alone changes the denominator and cannot estimate a canonical-versus-modified fraction. Request include_kmer=True for a k-mer mode with lexical tie breaking, or group_by_kmer=True to group by k-mer. Neither reconstruction nor mode calculation runs by default. Request mean_probabilities=True for supervised mean_probability_LABEL among called rows, using the stored class probabilities.

For supervised output with exactly two classes, set a binary decision threshold independently of row filters:

calls = open_output(output_dir)
sites = calls.summarize_loci(
    binary_threshold=0.8,
    binary_positive_class="5mC",  # Exact stored class label; required.
    include_class_counts=True,
    threads=4,
)

Each valid call becomes 5mC when P(5mC) >= 0.8, otherwise the other stored class (for example C). Both remain in called_count, so freq_5mC = count_5mC / called_count. For probabilities [0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9] at one site, count_5mC=2, called_count=4, and freq_5mC=0.5. Invalid probability rows stay no-calls and contribute only to total_count. The threshold accepts finite numbers in [0, 1], with an inclusive boundary. It requires exactly two classes in the selected probability source, even if classes requests only one report column. The positive class is explicit and does not depend on column order. Omitting both options preserves argmax.

This decision applies only to summary class counts/frequencies; it does not change read-level calls, stored probabilities, or probability means. The filters run first with their original semantics, including argmax-derived predicted_class and winning probability. Filtering on prob_5mC >= 0.8 would instead remove other reads from the denominator. The threshold supports both per-part aggregation and direct Parquet summary output.

Prototype summaries can additionally report frequencies within each canonical family and integer per-class counts:

sites = calls.summarize_loci(
    filters={"chrom": "chr2"},
    relative_frequencies=True,
    include_class_counts=True,
)

For 10 U calls, 10 pseU calls, 20 C calls, and 10 no-calls at one site, total_count=50, called_count=40, count_pseU=10, freq_pseU=0.25, and freq_pseU_rel=0.5. The relative denominator includes all called members of the U family, including other U modifications if present. It excludes other families and no-calls; zero family coverage produces null/NaN. These are prediction-family counts, not reference-base counts or deduplicated read IDs. Selecting classes=["pseU"] restricts reported columns without restricting the denominator. Read filters still change both denominators.

Both options default off. include_class_counts=True also works for supervised outputs. Effect split outputs supply family assignments in their manifest. Canonical T/U labels share a family. These options do not require reading scores, reconstructing k-mers, or loading read-level data into pandas.

Use mean_scores=True to add prototype mean_score_LABEL columns:

sites = calls.summarize_loci(
    classes=["pseU", "m6A"],
    include_class_counts=True,
    relative_frequencies=True,
    mean_scores=True,
)

mean_score_pseU averages the scores of calls predicted as pseU at that locus. It does not average pseU candidate scores from U or other predictions. Null, NaN and infinite scores are excluded from the mean without changing count_pseU; no finite pseU scores gives null/NaN. Filters apply before the mean, so a score threshold restricts the observations being averaged. The option defaults off; enabling it reads score payloads and retains bounded per-part aggregation, merging score sums and valid counts before division. Effect summaries use the winning-class score. Scores retain their original scorer semantics and are not converted to probabilities.

For canonical-null and pairwise summaries:

null_calls = open_output(null_output_dir)
sites = null_calls.summarize_loci(
    modified_pvalue_cutoff=0.05,
    min_pvalue=1e-300,
    # Optional additions; omit for the lightweight defaults:
    pvalue_thresholds=(0.001, 0.01, 0.05),
    confidence=0.95,
    metric_columns=["distance"],
    metric_stats=("mean", "std"),
    threads=4,
)

total_count counts finite p-values in [0, 1]; n_observations includes invalid p-values and n_invalid_p reports their count. fraction_modified uses the inclusive cutoff (p <= cutoff). combined_neglog10_pvalue uses Fisher's statistic with the given p-value floor/cap; zero valid observations produce null. Fisher combination defaults on for canonical-null and off for pairwise; combine_pvalues=True/False overrides this. Optional pvalue_thresholds add strict cutoff counts and fractions. confidence enables Wilson bounds for primary and extra fractions. Numeric summaries default off (metric_stats=()); request any of count, mean, std (sample deviation), or exact median. metric_columns selects metrics, otherwise available distances/PCs are discovered only when statistics are requested. Exact medians can require substantial memory. Uncalibrated null output without p-values returns observation counts plus requested numeric statistics. No conversion of anomaly fractions or Fisher significance into calibrated modification proportions is implied.

docs.title: Chemistry and signal preprocessing
docs.text: Checkpoint-based commands infer sequence type, pore chemistry, and expected k-mer current from the checkpoint. Do not supply --seq_type, --pore_type, or --kmer_dict_path in ordinary inference, fine-tuning, or embedding commands. If supplied, these options assert compatibility and fail on disagreement. Pretraining from scratch requires --chemistry or an explicit custom profile.

docs.title: Built-in profiles
docs.text:
Chemistry Sequence Expected-current table dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps DNA dna_r10.4.1_e8.2_400bps/9mer_levels_v1.txt rna004 RNA rna004/9mer_levels_v1.txt rna002 RNA rna_r9.4_180mv_70bps/5mer_levels_v1.txt

These files ship with PoreFM, pinned to nanoporetech/kmer_models commit 4e56daed7fbb79b538f58e41262d5c54b07356ea. Runtime use needs neither a separate checkout nor network access. Package metadata records upstream paths, file SHA-256 hashes, and hashes of the parsed float32 lookup values. Upstream license and copyright notices are included.

Identifiers and pore aliases are case-insensitive. RNA002 implies RNA; R9 plus seq_type="rna" also selects RNA002. Bare R9 is ambiguous and does not identify a table. Bare rna cannot distinguish RNA002 from RNA004. R10 plus DNA selects the registered 400-bps DNA profile.

RNA002 uses move-table decoding. Signal-based chunk inference remains restricted to 9-mer tables: provide BAM move tags and use mv, or auto with moves, for RNA002. Registering a chemistry does not make a pretrained backbone compatible with different signal widths or move strides.

docs.title: Python readers and datasets
docs.text:
Custom readers can use these exports without adopting PoreFM's dataset classes:

from porefm.data.bam import resolve_preprocessing, build_lookup_table, get_read_info_lite

prep = resolve_preprocessing(chemistry="rna002")
table = build_lookup_table(chemistry="rna002")  # Cached, read-only float32 array.
read_fields = get_read_info_lite(bam_record, preprocessing=prep)

Alternatively resolve from a trusted checkpoint without constructing a model:

from porefm.preprocessing import load_preprocessing
prep = load_preprocessing("model.pt")

All signal iterable datasets accept preprocessing=prep or one chemistry="rna004" argument. Model loading also exposes the resolved contract:

from porefm.models import load_model
from porefm.data.reader import BamIterableDataset

model = load_model("model.pt", model_type="backbone")
dataset = BamIterableDataset(
    bam_list=bam_list, size=2048, step=1792, move_downsample_factor=1,
    preprocessing=model.preprocessing,
)

Resolve once before the read loop. Collators that batch decoded samples need no table or chemistry arguments. Built-in tables retain upstream sequence orientation; BAM decoding reverses RNA signal into read orientation.

docs.title: Custom profiles and checkpoints
docs.text:
For an experiment with a custom table, provide its sequence type explicitly:

prep = resolve_preprocessing(
    chemistry="custom", seq_type="rna", pore_type="experimental",
    kmer_dict_path="my_levels.txt",
)

The headerless text format is KMER LEVEL, using a consistent odd k and ACGT encoding and finite current levels. build_lookup_table(path) returns a writable array; profile arrays are immutable. Custom checkpoints embed their exact table, so subsequent users do not need the original file.

When saving a custom model, include its resolved preprocessing profile and table so it can process signal on another machine. PoreFM checkpoint helpers use model.preprocessing. For a custom checkpoint writer, use attach_preprocessing(payload, prep) from porefm.preprocessing.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text:
Search or open an issue in the PoreFM issue tracker. Include the command, error traceback, PoreFM version or Git revision, model release, sequencing chemistry, GPU, and PyTorch/CUDA/FlashAttention versions. For input problems, describe whether you used BAM + POD5 or an SG-tagged BAM, and whether the reads were aligned and contained move tables.

A small reproducible example is helpful. Review logs and run_manifest.json before sharing them: manifests can contain local paths, hostnames, and input configuration snapshots.

docs.title: Cite PoreFM
docs.text:
Cite PoreFM as software using CITATION.cff. In a methods section, report:

  • The software version and Git revision.
  • The model repository and release tag, and checkpoint checksum when available.
  • Sequencing chemistry, target selection, read filters, and relevant scoring settings.
  • How read-level results were summarized, including coverage and decision thresholds.

Keep run_manifest.json with your results. Model downloads record the resolved release and checksum there. Cite the source datasets and reference assays separately; the HeLa example includes its GLORI and BACS references.

docs.text: PoreFM code is distributed under the MIT license. The vendored Oxford Nanopore k-mer resources retain their upstream license and copyright notices. Consult each model or dataset repository for the terms that apply to those separately distributed files.

docs.title: Other prototype scorers
docs.text:
For the released joint-footprinting model, use the prototype guide. This page covers alternative per-k-mer scorers and packaging custom artifacts.

For the per-k-mer scorers, porefm prototype classify fits one conditional classifier for every eligible k-mer. Classes are first partitioned by the canonical center base of their prototype k-mers, so only modifications applicable to the same center base are compared.

The command group also provides extract-kmer-prototypes, extract-effect-neighborhoods, and fit-effect-prototypes. Run porefm prototype --help to list them.

docs.title: Single-file model bundles
docs.text:
--model-path and --model_path accept either the usual pretrained checkpoint or a complete PoreFM inference bundle. A bundle selects its scorer and overrides separate --effect_model, --prototype_embeddings, and --class_labels arguments. The residual-effects bundle also ignores class-prior, metric, and classifier-output options belonging to other scorers. Runtime and input/output options remain available.

For a residual-effect model:

porefm utils bundle-model --kind prototype \
  --model_path pretraining/model.100 --effect_model neighbors.pt \
  --output RNA004_prototype.pt

porefm prototype classify --model-path RNA004_prototype.pt \
  --effect_penalty 50 \
  --bam_path reads.signal.bam --read_based --output_dir predictions

Effect penalty, neighbor selection, and decoder settings remain runtime options; the bundle does not save overrides for them. Omitting --effect_penalty retains the value saved in the fitted artifact. Other scorers can be packaged with --scorer, --prototype_embeddings and matching --class_labels instead of --effect_model. Their fitting and distance options remain inference CLI settings.

The destination must not exist. Bundles contain the inference backbone and fitted artifacts, so source files are not needed on the inference machine. Load a bundle with the inference CLI rather than torch.load. Inference verifies component checksums and extracts temporary copies under TMPDIR (or the system temporary directory). Allow space for the complete component set; the temporary files are cleaned up when inference exits.

docs.title: Per-k-mer scorers
docs.text:
Select a scorer with --scorer:

  • nearest-prototype: smallest raw cosine distance (default) or Euclidean distance selected with --metric l2. It uses saved exact means, with no temperature, covariance weighting, or prior adjustment. Ties select the first applicable class in --class_labels order.
  • centroid-l2: negative Euclidean distance divided by --score_temperature.
  • centroid-cosine: cosine similarity divided by --score_temperature.
  • centroid-rbf: negative squared Euclidean distance divided by twice --rbf_bandwidth squared.
  • diagonal-gaussian: class-specific feature variances estimated from each reservoir and shrunk toward one family-pooled feature variance using --diagonal_shrinkage.
  • per-kmer-lda: the full locally shrunk, shared-covariance LDA scorer.

The centroid, diagonal-Gaussian, and LDA scorers add the applicable class log-prior. Uniform priors are used unless --class_priors is supplied. Their Parquet outputs retain scores; they do not generate probabilities.

Nearest-prototype accepts omitted or uniform priors only; nonuniform priors are rejected. --metric is only valid with this scorer.

Nearest-prototype and centroid scorers consume the exact mean_embeddings and counts stored in a prototype file, so they also accept files extracted with --reservoir_size 0. Diagonal Gaussian and LDA require aligned reservoir embeddings, offsets, and counts. Supply these files with --prototype_embeddings.

Each prototype file must contain eligible k-mers with one canonical center base, and each family must have at least two classes. Within a family, only k-mers shared by all classes and meeting --min_prototype_count are scored. These requirements also apply to nearest-prototype; single-prototype and mixed-center inputs are not accepted.

docs.title: Read-based motifs and optional genome coordinates
docs.text:
Add --read_based (also spelled --read-based) to select targets from the called read sequence. Both --ref and --chrom are optional and can be used independently. Without --chrom, this mode streams mapped and unmapped primary records from unsorted/unindexed signal BAMs, with the usual read-quality, length and flag filters. With --chrom, only reads mapped to the requested contigs are fetched, requiring sorted, indexed signal BAMs. Direct BAM + POD5 uses a read-ID index instead. Raw signal is required through SG tags or --pod5; move tags are preferred, with inferred chunking available for supported chemistries. FASTQ or a basecall-only BAM without POD5 is insufficient.

By default it selects all canonical read bases (--motif 'N 0'). An explicit motif, such as --motif 'CG 0', is matched in the read sequence. Reference position files and reference-guided polishing cannot be combined with this mode. K-mer lookup and model inputs continue to use the called read sequence. The option supports all scorers, including residual-effects; fitted effect models can be reused without refitting.

read_pos is the zero-based index in the model's oriented read sequence. Supply --ref to retain zero-based genomic position coordinates on both strands. Motif matching still uses the read, even where it differs from the reference. For example, add these options to a classification command:

--read_based --motif 'A 0;C 0' --ref reference.fa --chrom chr1 chr2

Negative position values indicate absent reference coordinates: -1 for insertions/unmapped positions and -2 for soft clips. Unmapped records also have chrom='*' and strand=-1. Without --ref, mapped records retain their BAM chromosome/strand but their position is -1, including when --chrom filters the input. Use (readname, read_pos) to identify calls lacking genomic coordinates. Aligned mode requires both --ref and --chrom.

docs.title: Excluding genomic regions
docs.text:
Add --exclude-bed excluded.bed (or --exclude_bed excluded.bed) to porefm prototype classify. This uses the same whole-read exclusion as pairwise comparison, including all classifier scorers and residual-effects Parquet/BAM output. Exclusion defaults to disabled.

The file accepts chrom start end or chrom start end strand, with zero-based, half-open coordinates. Three-column rows exclude both strands; optional column 4 must be + or - and matches the BAM alignment strand, including for RNA:

chr9 3000000 3100000
chr9 5000000 5100000 -

Any matching overlap removes the entire query read before signal decoding, including calls outside the interval. The alignment span includes introns and deletions; touching endpoints do not overlap. Contig names must match the BAM. Blank lines and # comments are allowed. This is BED3 with an optional strand column, not standard BED4 names or BED6. See the pairwise exclusion documentation for the input format.

With --read_based, mapped reads can be filtered without --ref because the overlap uses BAM alignment coordinates; unmapped reads remain eligible. Saved prototype/effect artifacts are unaffected: this option filters the query BAMs. The BED path and SHA-256 are recorded in the run manifest.

docs.title: Output contract
docs.text:
The fitted artifact records format_version=4, the selected scorer_type, embedding method and dimension, k-mer size, global class order, center-base families, class priors, and scorer-specific fitted parameters.

For centroid, diagonal-Gaussian, and LDA scorers, each Parquet row contains:

  • score for the predicted class;
  • predicted_class_index and predicted_class;
  • score_<class> for every global class;
  • read, reference, strand, position, and k-mer identity columns.

Nearest-prototype instead writes distance, closest_prototype_index, closest_prototype, and distance_<class>, alongside the same identity and coordinate columns. Smaller distances are closer; no score or probability columns are emitted. Its fitted artifact also records the metric and means.

Only columns belonging to the query k-mer's center-base family are finite. Other class columns are NaN because those classes were not compared. Parquet output contains scores or distances, not probabilities.

For --scorer residual-effects, --output_format bam or both additionally supports RNA MM/ML output using conditional family softmax probabilities. parquet remains the default; other scorers support only Parquet. See effect BAM output for the SAM code table, temperature option, and probability semantics.

Run porefm prototype classify --help for the complete fitting and BAM query options.

docs.title: Context-conditioned effect model
docs.text:
Prototype models learn modification prototypes from small labelled datasets and use footprinting to account for neighboring effects when calling modifications. This page describes the fitted model and its scoring objective. To apply a released bundle, start with the prototype guide.

Task Reference Fit an artifact from matched modified and canonical samples Fit a custom effect model Score custom artifacts or tune memory and devices Scoring and resources Understand stored fields or write MM/ML BAM tags Output files and BAM tags Preview, filter, and summarize calls Output API

docs.title: Model and score
docs.text:
In the default recipe, for canonical base family b, fit the expected embedding μ_b(c) from canonical context means. A ridge regression on noncentral one-hot bases supplies an unseen context fallback. A supported exact context mean receives weight n/(n+s), where s is canonical_strength; the remainder is the regression prediction. The canonical context can be 9 bases even when effect training uses 5 bases.

In the default effect recipe, fit Δ_m(c) from matched modified–control means of the same k-mer, using equal-context ridge regression. effect_shrinkage blends this context-dependent prediction toward the global modification effect. There is no modified-target-context lookup in regression mode. Empirical and mixed modes instead retain and use the matched effect table. The center prototype is μ_b(query context) + Δ_m(query 5-mer). Different modifications retain different effect norms; weaker m6A separation is not normalized to match stronger effects.

Default canonical noise is pooled within context, centering each canonical reservoir group on its own sample mean. Its covariance is shrunk toward trace(Σ)/D times the identity, with an absolute diagonal floor. Row whitening is W=L^(-T), where LLᵀ=Σ. Both observations and candidate effects use the receiving base's W, or its receiving 5-mer's W in hierarchical mode. Modified reads never supply noise observations. This is vector whitening, not reuse of a scalar null z-score or an angular residual covariance in raw space.

Off-center templates F_m(offset, source flanks, receiving base) are fitted from paired modified/control reference-position means. All BED events in an oligo enter the additive design simultaneously. The separately fitted center effect is fixed and subtracted during this fit. A receiving-base-specific background absorbs sample-wide shifts and is not used as a biological footprint at inference. Footprint coefficients are shrunk toward an offset/receiving-base model without source-flank dependence. Offset zero is always reserved for Δ.

For a read configuration z (canonical or a compatible modification at each base), the relative score is:

Q(z) = -0.5 Σ_j ||(h_j - μ_j - Σ_i F_{z_i}(j-i)) W_j||²
       - penalty × number_of_modified_bases
       + 0.5 Σ_j ||(h_j - μ_j) W_j||²

F includes Δ at offset zero and is zero for canonical states. Pairwise overlap terms ensure each observation is used once in this objective. Finite-range beam search followed by alternating coordinate ascent approximates the best configuration. Multiple nearby modifications, including different types, are allowed; there is no one-modification-per-window constraint and no oracle event positions at inference. A reported class score holds the other inferred states fixed and compares the candidate center state against canonical.

This is a first-order additive model with independent receiving-position noise, not a learned model of modification–modification interactions or temporal noise covariance. Single-type oligos do not establish accuracy on mixed-modification reads. The beam search is approximate even when coordinate ascent converges.

docs.title: Evaluation considerations
docs.text: Before biological use, choose hyperparameters using held-out whole constructs and separate reads/samples, then freeze them. Compare center-only and neighbor models on identical callable positions; measure false positives by offset and base family, sensitivity separately for each modification, and performance on held-out IVT. Evaluate inferred-neighbor correction without using target BEDs as inference input. Mixed-modification nonadditivity, new 9-mer contexts, noisy basecalls, and sample-wide shifts need explicit validation. Synthetic checks alone do not establish held-out biological accuracy.

docs.title: Run output safety
docs.text:
By default, the following commands require an absent or empty output directory, or an absent output file. Hidden files, logs, and manifests count as existing results. Checks run before model loading and before opening logs or result writers.

Command Protected destination pretrain (including evaluation) --model_save_path finetune-modification (alias supervised-finetune) --model_save_path detect-modification (alias infer) --output zero-shot train / zero-shot train-scale --model_save_path when training zero-shot calibrate / zero-shot fit-whitening --calibration_output / --whitening_output zero-shot detect --output_dir prototype extract-kmer-prototypes (including union mode) --output, when supplied prototype extract-effect-neighborhoods, prototype fit-effect-prototypes --output prototype classify --output_dir and the fitted classifier file; includes residual-effects scoring python -m porefm.cli.single_read_tag Active Parquet --output and/or BAM --bam_output

Each output directory gets run_manifest.json. A standalone artifact also gets <filename>.run_manifest.json, allowing other artifacts to share its parent directory. Manifests record the invocation arguments, command, UTC time, host, working directory, canonical output paths, Git revision and dirty flags, input file sizes/mtimes, and JSON config snapshots with SHA-256 hashes. Large BAMs and checkpoints are not hashed. These are startup records, not completion markers; an interrupted run retains its reservation. Forced runs replace the manifests.

Supervised inference with direct sample options also records the normalized sample configuration, including defaults, in arguments.resolved_input. JSON input is captured as config snapshots. Both input routes retain the model release identity when using --model.

Distributed training/inference prepares outputs once on rank zero and broadcasts success or the error to every rank before writers or models start. The checks also apply when the canonical-null pipeline invokes its training and fitting stages directly. Its --force-overwrite flag is forwarded to executed stages. The pipeline's --skip_existing stage reuse takes precedence for completed stages; those stages are not executed or overwritten.

docs.title: Continuing training
docs.text:
Load a saved checkpoint using the command's loading/resume options, and choose a new --model_save_path, or explicitly pass --force-overwrite to reuse the existing directory. A checkpoint continuation still counts as a new invocation. Pretraining's --resume and --resume_interrupted_log retain their training/data-state semantics; they do not grant permission to reuse an occupied output directory.

Keep redirected stdout/stderr logs outside the run directory. For example, use a sibling run-name.log instead of run-name/train.log; the shell opens the log before Python checks the output directory.

docs.title: Explicit replacement
docs.text:
With --force-overwrite, the occupancy check still runs. If any destinations are occupied, a warning on stderr lists their paths before execution continues and permits matching files and run manifests to be overwritten directly. Fresh destinations produce no overwrite warning. Distributed runs print the warning once on rank zero. No backup or directory cleanup is performed. Unrelated files, stale result parts, and existing BAM indexes may remain; with this flag, managing those files and avoiding concurrent writers is the user's responsibility. The flag does not change the command's checkpoint-loading, resume, or training behavior.

The flag does not bypass checks for output symlinks, file/directory collisions, or destinations containing the working directory or repository. Direct output file aliases of discovered inputs are also rejected. Loading old-run/model.100 while writing to old-run is permitted with the flag: directory preparation leaves the checkpoint in place. Every destination is checked before any run manifests are written.

docs.title: Other workflows
docs.text: pairwise-comparison uses manifest-checked --resume behavior. Data conversion tools, plotting commands, and analysis scripts have their own output rules; the run-directory checks listed above do not apply to them. Check the relevant command or API before reusing an output path.

docs.title: Reuse the pretrained alignment
docs.text:
For a new cross-attention classifier initialized with --pretrain_load_path, add:

--classifier_type transformer_cross \
--classifier_center_source backbone

The default --classifier_center_source head learns a new center predictor during supervised fine-tuning. backbone consumes the u_center already returned by the final base-to-signal cross-attention layer and creates no classifier center predictor. The centers have shape (batch, base_tokens) and use signal-token coordinates, not raw sample or reference-genome coordinates. A backbone with only one base-to-signal layer returns static length-ratio centers; reuse uses those same returned values.

Both --classifier_signal_source fixed_sa_ts and contextual_ts preserve the signal-token axis and support reuse. Centers supply the distance penalty in attention scores; they do not force attention to one signal position or reuse the backbone's attention weights. The classifier still learns its query/key/ value projections, feed-forward network, optional mixer, and output layers.

The center input is detached. This prevents an additional classifier gradient through the reused center tensor, while ordinary gradients through base/signal embeddings follow the selected training policy. Use --freeze_pretrain to hold the entire backbone fixed; otherwise its centers can evolve as its weights change during fine-tuning or auxiliary pretraining.

The policy is recorded in classifier_config.center_source and the execution summary. Inference restores it automatically. Continuation with --model_load_path preserves it and rejects explicit policy changes. The option applies only to transformer_cross.

docs.title: Classifier precision and logit regularization
docs.text: See classifier numerical stability for the float32 final projections and losses, raw-logit penalty, and checkpoint metadata that records these policies.

docs.title: Interpret focal-loss probabilities
docs.text:
porefm.common.utils.focal_loss_fn first smooths targets toward uniform and then applies the per-class focal factor and alpha weight:

q_k = (1 - epsilon) * target_k + epsilon / K
loss = -sum_k alpha_k * q_k * (1 - p_k)^gamma * log(p_k)

Unlike ordinary cross entropy, this does not generally minimize at p=q. Even a small nonzero target on the incorrect class remains influential because its focal factor is large, while the correct class term is strongly downweighted as its predicted probability rises. Thus smoothing epsilon does not define the expected distance of a focal-loss confidence peak from zero or one. This is consistent with the probability-estimation analysis in Charoenphakdee et al., CVPR 2021.

For a controlled probability comparison, keep the same data, backbone training policy, and head while comparing cross entropy against focal loss. With focal loss, explicitly test zero smoothing for all classification sources. JSON sample settings override config settings, which override --label_smoothing, so a zero CLI fallback alone does not disable JSON overrides. Nonzero soft targets in label files still matter when the resolved epsilon is zero. See label-smoothing settings. Assess held-out log loss, Brier score, reliability by confidence bin, and discrimination. Fit any post-training calibration on a separate representative validation set.

docs.title: Assess head capacity
docs.text:
The cross head adds an attention block and inherits the backbone hidden width, attention-head count, and feed-forward width. --fc_dim_ff 32 only limits the final classification MLP; it does not shrink the attention block. Supervised training creates the head with zero dropout. Alignment reuse removes one predictor but leaves most of the head's capacity intact.

Compare CNN, cross attention with its own centers, and cross attention with reused centers using identical training data and loss settings. Start with a frozen backbone when isolating head capacity. Compare training and held-out performance, and hold out biological sources or sequence contexts where generalization is important. Overlapping chunks from the same reads/loci must not cross the split. Compressed probability peaks alone do not establish overfitting; a growing training/validation gap is more informative.

docs.title: Models API
docs.text:
Use load_model to load a local backbone, pretraining, or classifier checkpoint in Python. For complete analysis workflows and automatic model downloads, use the analysis guides.

from porefm.models import load_model

model = load_model("backbone.pt", model_type="backbone", device="cpu")
print(model.preprocessing)

By default the model is in evaluation mode with gradients disabled. For training, pass for_training=True when loading; calling model.train() alone does not re-enable gradients. Datasets can use model.preprocessing to match the checkpoint's signal processing; see preprocessing.

Single-file zero-shot and prototype bundles are loaded through their respective CLI commands. See model selection.

docs.title: porefm.models.load_model(checkpoint_path, *, model_type='auto', add_signal_cross_attn=None, include_ema=None, classifier_signal_source=None, for_training=False, device='cpu')
docs.text: Construct a PoreFM model directly from one trusted checkpoint path.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: checkpoint_path : str or pathlib.Path Pretraining, classifier, or backbone checkpoint. Checkpoints are loaded with pickle enabled and must therefore come from a trusted source. model_type : {"auto", "backbone", "pretraining", "classifier"}, default="auto" Model to construct. "auto" restores the complete declared model; "backbone" extracts only the shared backbone from any supported PoreFM checkpoint. add_signal_cross_attn : bool or None, default=None Preserve the checkpoint topology when None. False omits the signal-query-to-base cross-attention tower and contextual_ts while retaining base-query-to-signal attention and contextual base outputs. A tower absent from the checkpoint cannot be enabled. include_ema : bool or None, default=None For a pretraining model, None preserves the checkpoint's EMA setting and False omits the EMA encoder and latent head. Classifier inference omits auxiliary pretraining/EMA modules by default; passing True restores them when compatible weights are present. Backbones never construct EMA modules. classifier_signal_source : {"auto", "contextual_ts", "fixed_sa_ts"} or None Optional classifier-only signal source override. A classifier that requires contextual_ts cannot disable signal-to-base attention. for_training : bool, default=False If false, return an evaluation-mode model with gradients disabled. If true, return training mode with constructor-defined gradient settings, including a frozen EMA target. device : str or torch.device, default="cpu" Device receiving the constructed model after CPU checkpoint loading.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: torch.nn.Module An :class:ONTBackbone, :class:ONTModelForPreTraining, or :class:ONTModelForClassification according to model_type. model.preprocessing holds the resolved signal contract for use with datasets/readers, or None for checkpoints without identifying metadata. Signal workflows require an identified contract.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: ValueError If a requested component was not trained in the checkpoint or an option combination is incompatible with the requested model. RuntimeError If required checkpoint parameters are missing or unrelated unexpected parameters remain after applying an intentional topology reduction.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Use Linux with an NVIDIA GPU supported by FlashAttention 2, such as an A100, H100, RTX 3090, or RTX 4090. Python 3.12 is recommended. All four model workflows require CUDA-enabled PyTorch and FlashAttention.

docs.title: Set up GPU dependencies
docs.text:
In your Python environment, install PyTorch before FlashAttention. This setup uses PyTorch 2.10.0 with CUDA 12.8 and FlashAttention 2.8.3. Skip these steps if you already have these versions working.

python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel packaging ninja psutil
python -m pip install torch==2.10.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python -m pip install flash-attn==2.8.3 --no-build-isolation

The CUDA wheel must be compatible with your NVIDIA driver; see the official PyTorch installation options. Install FlashAttention after selecting PyTorch, because its compiled extension must match that environment. --no-build-isolation lets its installer use the PyTorch you just installed.

FlashAttention attempts to use a matching prebuilt wheel when available. Plan for a source build with the PyTorch 2.10 / CUDA 12.8 combination above, unless a compatible cached or separately supplied wheel is available. The upstream release includes PyTorch 2.10 wheels labelled cu13; those target CUDA 13 and do not match this CUDA 12.8 setup. Compilation can take a long time. See the official wheel list and the build guidance below.

docs.title: Install PoreFM
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/WGLab/PoreFM.git
cd PoreFM
python -m pip install .

Pip installs the remaining Python dependencies, including those used to read, summarize, and plot outputs. For an editable installation, use python -m pip install -e . instead.

Input preparation also uses the external samtools command. Install it through your system or cluster package manager and check that samtools --version works. Model files are supplied separately.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
Run this on a machine with an allocated GPU:

porefm --help
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import flash_attn

print("PyTorch:", torch.__version__, "CUDA:", torch.version.cuda)
print("FlashAttention:", flash_attn.__version__)
assert torch.cuda.is_available(), "No CUDA GPU is visible to PyTorch"
print("GPU:", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))
PY

docs.title: If FlashAttention needs to compile
docs.text:
Source builds require a CUDA toolkit with nvcc and a C++ compiler. Use a toolkit matching the CUDA version of PyTorch (12.8 for the command above). The CUDA runtime in a PyTorch wheel does not provide the nvcc compiler. On a cluster, load the appropriate CUDA module for your system before building.

To limit build memory use, cap the number of compiler jobs:

MAX_JOBS=4 python -m pip install flash-attn==2.8.3 --no-build-isolation

Leave FLASH_ATTENTION_FORCE_BUILD unset for normal installation: setting it to TRUE forces compilation even if a matching wheel exists. Keep pip's cache enabled so subsequent installs can reuse a built wheel. A prebuilt wheel must match Python, PyTorch, CUDA, the platform, and the C++ ABI; a wheel for another PyTorch version is not interchangeable. See the FlashAttention installation guide.

Continue with the HeLa RNA example for a first result using downloadable data, or prepare your own inputs.

docs.title: Export per-base embeddings
docs.text: Use PoreFM embeddings for your own exploratory analyses or downstream models. This recipe exports representations for two aligned populations using the same collector as pairwise comparison. It needs the sorted, indexed signal BAMs and reference described in input preparation.

docs.title: Export an RNA region
docs.text:
porefm pairwise-comparison \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA@v0.1.0 \
  --control-bam signal/control.signal.bam \
  --test-bam signal/test.signal.bam \
  --ref reference.fa --chrom-list chr3 \
  --embedding-key contextual_base_seq \
  --store-embeddings --block-size 1000 \
  --forward-batch-size 16 \
  --output outputs/embeddings

Replace chr3 with a contig in your inputs. contextual_base_seq is the signal-contextualized representation at each base. Its width is 512 for the released RNA backbone and 384 for the DNA backbone. Select a chemistry-matched checkpoint from Models.

--store-embeddings can run alone, as above, or accompany the scoring flags in the pairwise guide. Export alone does not produce anomaly p-values. Eligible observations are assigned to one overlapping chunk, using the greatest distance from its sequence edges, so a read position contributes at most once. Input filters still apply; the export is not an unfiltered copy of BAM depth.

docs.title: Inspect a saved block
docs.text:
Files are written under outputs/embeddings/embeddings/. Each .pt file covers a genomic block and stores control, test, control_summary, and test_summary, together with the chromosome and representation name.

from pathlib import Path
import torch
import pandas as pd

path = next(Path("outputs/embeddings/embeddings").glob("*.pt"))
# These locally generated blocks contain NumPy metadata as well as tensors.
block = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
rows = block["test"]
print(block["chrom"], block["embedding_key"])
print(rows["embeddings"].shape)  # (observations, embedding_dimension)

preview = pd.DataFrame({
    "readname": rows["readnames"][:5],
    "position": rows["positions"][:5].numpy(),
    "read_pos": rows["read_positions"][:5].numpy(),
    "strand": rows["strands"][:5].numpy(),
})
print(preview)
features = rows["embeddings"][:5].float().numpy()
print(features.shape)

Load only trusted .pt files. Observation embeddings are stored as bfloat16; convert selected rows to float32 before passing them to NumPy-based tools. Site summaries store float32 means, integer counts, positions, and strands. Reference positions are zero-based, strand is 0 forward/1 reverse, and read_positions follow the collector's oriented read sequence.

Process one block at a time to limit memory use. Keep biological sources or reads separate when constructing training and evaluation sets. Distances and clusters in this representation do not themselves establish modification identity. For loading a checkpoint in custom Python code, see the model API.

docs.title: Prepare inputs and models
docs.text: The application guides use RNA004 examples and supplied, already trained models. Start with an aligned basecall BAM, its original POD5 signal, and the same reference FASTA used for alignment. Replace the example filenames with your own files. Run commands from your analysis directory in Bash, with PoreFM installed and your GPU environment active.

docs.title: Choose the input path
docs.text:
Aligned basecalls.bam + original POD5 signal + reference.fa
    |
    +-- read directly --------------------> Supervised detection
    |                                  +--> Zero-shot detection
    |                                  +--> Residual prototype scoring
    |
    +-- attach signal --> sort --> index -> Pairwise comparison
                          signal.bam       (test and control)

An ordinary basecall BAM alone does not contain the raw signal PoreFM needs. For the first three guides, PoreFM joins BAM records to POD5 reads by read ID. --pod5 accepts one file or a directory searched recursively. Supervised detection also accepts these inputs through JSON. Use one BAM and one POD5 source per run, without duplicated read IDs across POD5 files.

Direct BAM + POD5 input does not require a coordinate-sorted BAM or a BAI/CSI index. PoreFM creates or reuses a read-ID index (.pfmi) automatically. Keep the alignment in the BAM to obtain reference-site summaries.

Index the reference once:

samtools faidx reference.fa

The reference sequence names must match the BAM. The examples keep outputs under outputs/ and summaries under summaries/. Choose a fresh output directory for each run; see output safeguards.

docs.title: Move tables
docs.text:
Include --emit-moves when basecalling with Dorado and preserve the resulting mv tags during alignment. These tags describe how basecalls map to signal steps; see Dorado's move-table documentation.

PoreFM's default chunking uses move tables when present. Without them, direct BAM + POD5 inference can infer chunks heuristically from the sequence and signal. This fallback has given similar results in our analyses, but it does not guarantee identical calls. These guides use RNA004; the RNA002 profile requires move tables. See preprocessing for details.

docs.title: Choose a model
docs.text:
The analysis guides use --model OWNER/REPOSITORY@vVERSION, for example --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0. PoreFM downloads the matching checkpoint once, verifies its SHA-256, and reuses its local cache. No Hugging Face login or package is required. See Models for releases, checksums, cache configuration, and prefetching for offline jobs.

You can instead supply a local checkpoint with --model-path or --model_path. For example, a manually downloaded RNA model directory might contain:

models/
|-- supervised/model.pt      # Complete modification classifier
|-- RNA004_zero-shot.pt      # Backbone, null/scale models, whitening, calibration
|-- RNA004_prototype.pt      # Backbone and fitted residual effects
`-- backbone.pt              # Pretrained backbone for pairwise comparison

The released checkpoints supply sequence type, pore chemistry, and expected k-mer currents through metadata. The classifier also supplies its canonical base, class labels, and modification codes. The recipes therefore need no manual chemistry, k-mer-table, or modification-code arguments.

Zero-shot and prototype bundles contain their matching model components. Separate-file inputs remain supported for custom models: keep zero-shot artifacts from the same release together, and pair fitted residual effects with their exact backbone checkpoint. A model trained for a different chemistry is not a drop-in replacement.

docs.title: Prepare signal BAMs for pairwise comparison
docs.text:
Skip this step for the three direct BAM + POD5 guides. For pairwise comparison, prepare one signal BAM for each population. Here control.bam and test.bam are aligned basecall BAMs, with their POD5 files in corresponding directories.

The current pod5-to-bam converter requires move tables and skips reads without mv tags. Use basecalls produced with --emit-moves for this step.

mkdir -p signal
for sample in control test; do
  porefm utils pod5-to-bam \
    --bam "${sample}.bam" --input "pod5/${sample}" \
    --output signal --prefix "${sample}.unsorted" --threads 4
  samtools sort -@ 4 -o "signal/${sample}.signal.bam" \
    "signal/${sample}.unsorted.bam"
  samtools index "signal/${sample}.signal.bam"
done

Signal attachment writes an unsorted BAM containing SG signal tags. Sorting and indexing make it ready for the coordinate-based pairwise workflow. Keep both populations aligned to the same reference.

Continue with supervised detection, zero-shot detection, pairwise comparison, or residual prototype scoring.

docs.title: Process output files
docs.text:
All four guides use the same Python entry point, porefm.outputs.open_output. It reads saved predictions without loading model weights or using a GPU. Use a completed run directory and keep data/meta pairs and manifests together.

completed run directory
        |
        v
   open_output
        |
        +--> iter_tables ------> preview/filter individual read observations
        |
        `--> summarize_loci ---> one row per chromosome, position, strand
                                  |
                                  `--> summary Parquet for plots/analysis

docs.title: Preview a few observations
docs.text:
from porefm.outputs import open_output

calls = open_output("outputs/zero-shot")
print(calls.format)
print(calls.schema.names)
for table in calls.iter_tables(batch_size=5):
    print(table.to_pandas())
    break

Change the path to outputs/supervised, outputs/pairwise, or outputs/residual to inspect another guide's result. Opening a pairwise run selects read_scores/; its companion site tables are read separately.

docs.title: Choose the right site summary
docs.text:
Workflow What the summary measures Example Supervised Hard class counts/fractions, optionally mean class probabilities Supervised summary Zero-shot Fraction of valid calls with a small canonical-null p-value Zero-shot summary Pairwise Fraction of valid test calls that deviate from the control Pairwise summary Residual prototypes Hard class counts, including within-family fractions Residual summary

The snippets in those guides write directly to a summary Parquet instead of loading all read observations into RAM. Use a new summary filename for each analysis. The default memory budget is 8 GB; memory_limit and temp_directory can be set for larger runs.

To preview a saved summary:

import pyarrow.parquet as pq

summary = pq.ParquetFile("summaries/zero-shot.parquet")
for batch in summary.iter_batches(batch_size=5):
    print(batch.to_pandas())
    break

docs.title: Coordinates and denominators
docs.text:
Reference position is zero-based. strand is 0 for forward, 1 for reverse. read_pos follows the producer's oriented read sequence; it is not a genomic coordinate. Site summaries exclude observations without valid reference coordinates. They summarize retained predictions, so coverage can be lower than BAM depth after input filtering, context checks, or edge trimming.

Filter by region when needed, but retain the calls that form the denominator:

sites = calls.summarize_loci(
    filters=[("chrom", "==", "chr3"),
             ("position", ">=", 1_000_000),
             ("position", "<", 1_010_000)],
    modified_pvalue_cutoff=0.01,
)
print(sites.head())

This small-region example applies to the zero-shot run opened above. For anomaly fractions, retain both significant and nonsignificant p-values. For class fractions, retain canonical and modified calls. Filtering to positive calls first makes the resulting fraction misleading.

The name fraction_modified in anomaly summaries means the fraction passing the chosen p-value cutoff, not a calibrated biological modification fraction. Likewise, effect scores and supervised probabilities have different meanings and should not be compared as if they were the same quantity.

For selected columns, read filters, DuckDB queries, and detailed schemas, see the output API reference.

docs.title: Compare a test sample with a control
docs.text:
Use this recipe when you have a matched control population, such as an IVT RNA control, and want to measure how a test sample differs at the same reference positions. It produces both per-test-read anomaly scores and differences between the mean test and control embeddings.

Follow input and model preparation. You need sorted, indexed signal/control.signal.bam and signal/test.signal.bam, and reference.fa with its .fai. Both BAMs must contain raw signal (SG tags). The command downloads and caches the backbone from WGLab/PoreFM-RNA@v0.1.0. See Models to prefetch it for offline use.

control.signal.bam --+
                    +--> same backbone --> embeddings at each position/strand
test.signal.bam -----+                           |
                         +----------------------+---------------------+
                         |                                            |
                    mean embeddings                            joint local PCA
                         |                                     + control null
                  test/control shift                                  |
                         |                                  test-read p-values
                         v                                            v
                  locus_metrics/                                read_scores/
                                                     + anomaly_site_metrics/

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
This example processes chr3. Set --chrom-list to the contigs of interest in your BAM and reference.

porefm pairwise-comparison \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA@v0.1.0 \
  --control-bam signal/control.signal.bam \
  --test-bam signal/test.signal.bam \
  --ref reference.fa --chrom-list chr3 \
  --sitewise-anomaly-scoring --sitewise-embedding-shift \
  --output outputs/pairwise

--sitewise-anomaly-scoring scores individual test reads against the control. --sitewise-embedding-shift also measures the difference between the two populations' mean embeddings. Both operate at matching reference positions and strands, without a motif restriction. For a local checkpoint, replace --model with --model-path models/backbone.pt.

The basic command requires at least 15 retained observations per population at a site. See the pairwise reference for coverage settings and multiple BAM inputs.

docs.title: Read both types of results
docs.text:
outputs/pairwise/
|-- read_scores/              # Paired data/meta Parquets for test reads
|-- locus_metrics/            # Mean test/control embedding differences
|-- anomaly_site_metrics/     # Coverage and fitted PCA/null statistics
`-- run_manifest.json

Summarize test-read anomalies after the comparison completes:

from pathlib import Path
from porefm.outputs import open_output

Path("summaries").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
calls = open_output("outputs/pairwise")
calls.summarize_loci(
    modified_pvalue_cutoff=0.01,
    output_path="summaries/pairwise.parquet",
    threads=4,
)

# Preview the separately computed site-level embedding shifts.
for table in calls.iter_site_tables(kind="locus_metrics", batch_size=5):
    print(table.to_pandas())
    break

Here fraction_modified means the fraction of retained, valid test-read p-values at each site that are <= 0.01. It measures disagreement with the control, not the identity or stoichiometry of a modification. Experimental differences between populations can also create a shift. The companion site tables retain the original comparison statistics; later filtering of read scores does not refit them.

See processing outputs for coordinates and read-level previews.

docs.title: Optional settings
docs.text:
Expanded command with window, filtering, and resource settings

This alternative requires 30 observations per population and fits on up to 512 observations from each. It uses two principal components and a chi-square null. PCA is fitted separately at each position and strand, so PC coordinates cannot be compared across sites.

The command also changes signal windows and read-quality filtering. Batch size, worker count, and block size control resource use; reduce --forward-batch-size if GPU memory is limiting.

porefm pairwise-comparison \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA@v0.1.0 \
  --embedding-key contextual_base_seq \
  --control-bam signal/control.signal.bam \
  --test-bam signal/test.signal.bam \
  --ref reference.fa --chrom-list chr3 \
  --sitewise-anomaly-scoring --sitewise-embedding-shift \
  --min-control-coverage 30 --min-test-coverage 30 \
  --max-fit-coverage 512 --n-components 2 --pvalue-method chi2 \
  --size 4096 --step 3600 --num-trim 8 \
  --block-size 1000 --min-read-length 100 --min-qscore 0 \
  --forward-batch-size 16 --num-workers 1 --compile-model \
  --output outputs/pairwise

docs.title: Prototype-based joint footprinting
docs.text:
Call modifications using prototypes learned from small labelled datasets. The model uses footprinting to account for neighboring modification effects when assigning classes. The released prototype models support a broader set of modifications than the supervised classifiers, including types without a supervised model; see the model catalog.

This guide uses the released RNA model with the residual-effects scorer, neighbor effects enabled, and a modification penalty of 50.

The canonical baseline, noise model, and modification effects shown at the top are already fitted in the released bundle. The command below performs scoring.

Follow input and model preparation. You need basecalls.bam, pod5/, and reference.fa with its .fai. The command downloads and caches WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0, which contains the backbone and matching fitted effects. No prototype extraction or fitting is needed. See Models to prefetch it for offline use.

basecalls.bam + POD5 --> backbone --> observed embeddings
                                            |
fitted effects --> expected canonical baseline + modification effects
                                            |
                        residuals measured using canonical noise
                                            |
                      jointly score center and neighboring states
                              (modification penalty = 50)
                                            |
                         per-base class calls + relative scores
                                            |
                          class frequencies at reference sites

The effect artifact supplies the canonical baseline, noise model, supported classes, and modification footprints. It must match the exact backbone used when it was fitted. Neighbor scoring helps explain a perturbation across several bases without treating every affected base as a separate event.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
This example scores chr1. Replace it with the contig names in your BAM and reference; --chrom accepts more than one name.

porefm prototype classify \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0 \
  --effect_penalty 50 \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ --ref reference.fa \
  --chrom chr1 --motif 'N 0' \
  --output_dir outputs/residual

N 0 selects all eligible aligned bases. Neighbor effects and GPU scoring are enabled by default. The penalty of 50 is part of this supplied RNA recipe; it is not a p-value, an FDR threshold, or a universal setting for other models. The bundle selects the residual-effects scorer. For a local bundle, replace --model with --model-path models/RNA004_prototype.pt.

docs.title: Summarize calls within each base family
docs.text:
outputs/residual/
|-- part_*_data.parquet       # Class calls and family-local scores
|-- part_*_meta.parquet       # Read and alignment metadata
|-- effect_parts.json        # Output parts, classes, completion state
|-- effect_run.json          # Effect model and scoring settings
|-- run_manifest.json
`-- *.pfmi                   # Automatic BAM read-ID index, if needed

After classification finishes:

from pathlib import Path
from porefm.outputs import open_output

Path("summaries").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
calls = open_output("outputs/residual")
calls.summarize_loci(
    relative_frequencies=True,
    include_class_counts=True,
    output_path="summaries/residual.parquet",
    threads=4,
)

count_LABEL counts hard class calls. freq_LABEL_rel divides a class count by all called predictions in its canonical-plus-modified family: for example, an A modification is divided by A and all modeled A modifications. The actual labels and families come from the artifact. A family with no calls has a null relative frequency. freq_LABEL instead divides by all called classes at the site.

Keep canonical calls in these denominators. Unsupported contexts can produce no-calls, so inspect called_count alongside total_count. Stored effect scores compare classes given inferred neighbors; they are not calibrated probabilities.

See processing outputs for common operations and the effect-model reference for scoring details.

docs.title: Optional settings
docs.text:
Expanded command with window, filtering, and resource settings

This Bash example reads every reference contig from the FASTA index and sets signal windows, read filtering, and resource limits explicitly.

Batch size, workers, cache, block, and queue sizes control resource use. The effect cache alone can use up to 4096 MiB here; reduce --effect_cache_mb and --batch_size on smaller GPUs. Beam width and sweep count control the approximate search for joint class assignments.

REF=reference.fa
mapfile -t CHROMS < <(cut -f1 "${REF}.fai")

porefm prototype classify \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_prototype@v0.1.0 \
  --effect_neighbors on --effect_penalty 50 \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ --ref "$REF" \
  --chrom "${CHROMS[@]}" --motif 'N 0' \
  --size 4096 --step 3400 --num_trim 8 \
  --min_qscore 0 --min_read_length 100 \
  --batch_size 64 --reads_per_chunk 10 \
  --num_workers 4 --prefetch_factor 4 \
  --device cuda --effect_device cuda \
  --effect_cache_mb 4096 --effect_threads 4 \
  --effect_beam_width 32 --effect_max_sweeps 8 \
  --effect_block_size 4096 --effect_queue_size 8 --effect_queue_mb 512 \
  --seed 0 --log_every 100 \
  --output_dir outputs/residual

docs.title: Supervised modification detection
docs.text:
Use a supplied fine-tuned classifier to call its trained modification classes from contextual PoreFM representations. RNA classifiers are available for m6A/inosine and pseudouridine; see Models for supported classes. The first recipe scores A positions in the called read sequence and writes both read-level Parquet predictions and a BAM with modification tags.

First follow input and model preparation. You need basecalls.bam, pod5/, and reference.fa with its .fai. The command downloads and caches WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine@v0.1.0. See Models to prefetch it for offline use.

basecalls.bam + POD5
        |
        v
  signal/sequence chunks
        |
        v
  fine-tuned classifier <--- model.pt (weights + class metadata)
        |
        +--> output.bam                 MM/ML modification tags
        `--> prediction Parquets -----> class counts/fractions at each site
                              reference.fa supplies aligned coordinates

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
Provide the sample directly on the command line:

porefm detect-modification \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ \
  --read_based --ref reference.fa --motif 'A 0' \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine@v0.1.0 \
  --output_format both \
  --output outputs/supervised

--read_based selects motifs in basecalls, and --ref retains available genomic coordinates for aligned reads. A 0 selects the A itself. Use a selector appropriate to the released model's target base. For an SG-tagged signal BAM, omit --pod5.

The checkpoint supplies preprocessing settings, class labels, the canonical base, and modification codes. --output_format both writes predictions and a BAM with modification tags. For a local checkpoint, replace --model with --model-path models/supervised/model.pt; --model_load_path remains supported.

Without --read_based, targets come from the reference: supply --ref and either --motif or --pos_file. Use --contigs chr1 chr2 (also --chrom) to restrict contigs. Direct sample options accept hyphenated spellings too, such as --bam-path, --read-based, and --pos-file.

Relative input paths are resolved from the directory where you run the command. run_manifest.json records the direct options and their normalized defaults in arguments.resolved_input, alongside the model release provenance.

docs.title: Pseudouridine detection
docs.text:
Use the pseU model to classify canonical U versus pseudouridine in RNA004 reads:

porefm detect-modification \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ \
  --read_based --ref reference.fa --motif 'T 0' \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_pseU@v0.1.0 \
  --output_format both \
  --output outputs/supervised-pseu

RNA uridine is encoded as T in BAM sequences, so target T 0 even though the model's canonical class is named U. The saved class order is U, pseU; the checkpoint supplies base T and modification code 17802 for BAM tags. Keep each classifier's output in its own directory. The HeLa walkthrough shows both models and plots their calls together.

docs.title: JSON input alternative
docs.text:
JSON configs remain supported. Save the following as sample.json for the same sample and A-base target selection as the first command:

{
  "config_type": "supervised",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "labelled_samples": [
    {
      "bam_path": "basecalls.bam",
      "pod5": "pod5/",
      "read_based": true,
      "ref": "reference.fa",
      "motif": "A 0"
    }
  ]
}

labelled_samples selects prediction targets; known modification labels are not required for inference.

porefm detect-modification \
  --bam_config sample.json \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine@v0.1.0 \
  --output_format both \
  --output outputs/supervised

Use either --bam_config or direct sample settings. They share validation and defaults, and cannot be mixed. The global --read_based override for JSON configs remains supported. JSON is useful for multiple samples with different settings or tagged label sources. Multiple SG BAMs with shared settings can also be passed as --bam_path first.bam second.bam; POD5 input requires one BAM file. See the input option mapping for additional filters and polishing options.

docs.title: Read the results
docs.text:
outputs/supervised/
|-- output.bam
|-- checkpoint_*_data.parquet  # Position-level logits and probabilities
|-- checkpoint_*_meta.parquet  # Read identities and alignment metadata
|-- run_manifest.json
`-- *.pfmi                    # Automatic BAM read-ID index, if needed

Keep each data/meta pair together. The BAM produced from POD5 input is unsorted. For coordinate-based viewers or downstream tools, create a sorted, indexed copy:

samtools sort -@ 4 -o outputs/supervised/calls.sorted.bam \
  outputs/supervised/output.bam
samtools index outputs/supervised/calls.sorted.bam

After inference finishes, summarize the Parquets without loading a model:

from pathlib import Path
from porefm.outputs import open_output

Path("summaries").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
calls = open_output("outputs/supervised")
calls.summarize_loci(
    include_class_counts=True,
    mean_probabilities=True,
    output_path="summaries/supervised.parquet",
    threads=4,
)

Each reference site has called_count, count_LABEL, and freq_LABEL columns using the checkpoint's actual labels. Frequencies count the most probable class per call; mean probabilities are a separate statistic. Retain canonical and modified calls when computing fractions. These are model call fractions, not automatically calibrated modification stoichiometry.

See processing outputs for previews, coordinates, and filtering.

docs.title: Optional settings
docs.text:
Expanded command with window, filtering, and resource settings

Use this alternative when you want explicit signal windows and more loader workers. It also disables the default minimum read quality and length filters, so its retained calls can differ from the basic command.

--size, --step, and --num_trim set signal windows and edge trimming. --batch_size, --reads_per_chunk, and loader settings control resource use; reduce the batch size if GPU memory is limiting. --checkpoint_batch_step controls prediction writes, not model checkpoints.

porefm detect-modification \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ \
  --read_based --ref reference.fa --motif 'A 0' \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_m6A-Inosine@v0.1.0 \
  --size 4096 --step 3400 --num_trim 8 \
  --checkpoint_batch_step 500 --reads_per_chunk 10 \
  --dataloader_workers 8 --batch_size 256 --prefetch_factor 2 \
  --min_qscore 0 --min_read_length 0 \
  --output_format both \
  --output outputs/supervised

docs.title: Zero-shot detection with a canonical reference
docs.text:
Use this recipe to find read positions that deviate from the supplied canonical RNA model. It uses a fitted null predictor, whitening transform, scale model, and calibration. You do not need a control sample at inference time or modification-labelled training data for your sample.

The training and fitting steps in the top row are already completed in the released bundle. You only need to run detection on your sample.

Follow input and model preparation. Supply basecalls.bam, pod5/, and reference.fa with its .fai. The command downloads and caches WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_zero-shot@v0.1.0, which contains all matching model components. See Models to prefetch it for offline use.

basecalls.bam + POD5 --> backbone --> observed embedding
                                         |
sequence context --> null predictor --> expected canonical embedding
                                         |
                         observed minus expected
                                         |
                              whitening.pt
                                         |
                             residual distance
                                         |
                                scale model
                                         |
                            normalized anomaly score
                                         |
                               calibration.pt
                                         |
                              per-base p-value
                                         |
                         anomaly fraction at each site

The zero-shot bundle contains every model component shown above.

Whitening accounts for canonical residual variability. The scale model accounts for context-dependent score variation; calibration converts scores to tail p-values against the canonical reference. A small p-value indicates a deviation, not a named modification or the probability of modification.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
porefm zero-shot detect \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ \
  --ref reference.fa --motif "N 0" \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_zero-shot@v0.1.0 \
  --output_dir outputs/zero-shot

N 0 selects all eligible aligned bases across reference contigs. Calibration metadata in the bundle selects the score type automatically. For a local bundle, replace --model with --model-path models/RNA004_zero-shot.pt.

docs.title: Summarize anomalies at reference sites
docs.text:
outputs/zero-shot/
|-- part_*_data.parquet       # Position, distance, score, p-value
|-- part_*_meta.parquet       # Read and alignment metadata
|-- run_manifest.json
`-- *.pfmi                   # Automatic BAM read-ID index, if needed

The basic command writes calls with raw distance greater than zero. To retain a broad range of distances for site fractions, add --min_metric -1000 to the detection command. Avoid restricting detection output to significant calls or peaks: that removes calls needed for the denominator.

After detection finishes:

from pathlib import Path
from porefm.outputs import open_output

Path("summaries").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
calls = open_output("outputs/zero-shot")
calls.summarize_loci(
    modified_pvalue_cutoff=0.01,
    metric_columns=["distance"],
    metric_stats=["mean"],
    output_path="summaries/zero-shot.parquet",
    threads=4,
)

total_count counts retained valid p-values at a site. fraction_modified is the output API's name for the fraction with p <= 0.01: interpret it as an anomaly fraction, not modification stoichiometry. The summary also includes mean distance and, by default, a Fisher combined p-value. Fisher combination assumes independent observations; it does not identify the chemical modification responsible for a signal change.

See processing outputs for common operations and zero-shot reference for specialized filtering.

docs.title: Optional settings
docs.text:
Expanded command with window, filtering, and resource settings

Use this alternative for explicit signal windows, additional loader workers, and broader read/call retention. --min_qscore 0 disables the default read quality filter; --min_metric -1000 retains a broad range of raw distances. These settings affect which calls enter downstream summaries.

Worker count and prefetch depth control input throughput. Checkpoint and log intervals control output writes and progress reporting.

porefm zero-shot detect \
  --bam_path basecalls.bam --pod5 pod5/ \
  --ref reference.fa --motif "N 0" \
  --model WGLab/PoreFM-RNA_zero-shot@v0.1.0 \
  --score_type auto \
  --size 4096 --step 3400 --num_trim 8 \
  --num_workers 4 --prefetch_factor 4 \
  --min_metric -1000 --min_qscore 0 \
  --checkpoint_batch_step 100 --log_every 100 \
  --output_dir outputs/zero-shot

docs.title: Signal chunking
docs.text: For ordinary inference, keep the default auto mode. This reference explains when to select another method and how boundaries affect model inputs.

docs.title: Chunk-boundary selection
docs.text:
Data-consuming commands expose --chunking_mode auto|mv|hierarchical|dtw|inferred. Omission defaults to auto: use move-based decoding when mv exists, hierarchical anchors for DNA without moves, and mean6 DTW for RNA without moves. Auto does not hide errors in malformed present move tags.

Explicit mv requires move tags. Explicit hierarchical or dtw forces that method for either DNA or RNA, even when moves exist.

Alternatively, pass --chunking_config /path/to/chunking.json with:

{"chunking_mode": "dtw"}

This is a separate, run-wide data-processing JSON file, not a BAM manifest or model configuration. An explicit --chunking_mode overrides the JSON value.
